Great relatively inexpensive television. I did not have any kind of line at the bottom (which one of the other reviewers had experienced). This is a very light set and I was easily able to maneuver the box inside and set up all by myself. The picture is crystal clear and the contrast is simply remarkable at a price like this. I set this up in my bedroom and was super impressed with the quality of this Polaroid television. I am sure the reason for the lightweight feature of this television may largely be due to plastic pieces, but I don't notice it when set up. I also find the sound quality of this set impressive, too (no need for me to attach my sound bar). All and all, very impressed. If the price on this goes down even further over the holidays, I would jump on it. I will be keeping my out for the sales as I would love to get one for my son.

PLEASE PLEASE, do not buy these cameras and the doorbell. I did not listen. Now I am not going to use a lot of big words to describe the problem. I am just going to tell you the truth. I am 70 years old and I purchased these cameras because I live alone and I wanted security. I am not secure and I do not feel secure. I purchased due to all the advertisements and because Shaq endorsed them. They do not work and the customer service really sucks. One day I was put on hold for 45 minutes then hung up on. The supervisors are no help at all. I purchased 3 floodlight cameras and 1 doorbell camera. They all are malfunctioning. The doorbell does not alert until the person is long gone. What is the purpose if the incident is over before you can even see it. Then you cannot even pull the incident up for about 4-5 minutes! You have to wait to see who was at your door and that's not safe. in 4-5 minutes someone could already be in your house!! I have horrible neighbors who are interfering with one of the floodlight cameras and literally making it go off every 1-3 minutes. I've called ring over 52 times since October of 2019. They cannot or will not resolve the issue, other than tell me the camera cannot be tampered with. I KNOW THAT IS NOT CORRECT! If you buy these cameras buy at your own risk. I am here to tell you that they do not work and customer service will not help you when they fail and they will fail!!!! Shame on you Shaq O' Neal. Shame on you Amazon for buying and selling this mess !!!!!!!  On my last recent call to Ring I was told that the cameras do not work in real time. The representatives say whatever they want to try and get you to hang up. I'm 70 not senile. Someone named Richmond told me that! The commercials show the people walking up, you activating the sound and talking to the person. One of My problems is the people are already gone before the camera actually activates. I would look into buying something else if I could afford it. You have a choice. DO NOT BUY RING. Do not be tricked like I was.

I am going to provide a list of pros and cons... but to summarize, I am really disappointed. The most disappointing thing... a HUGE BLACK box that you must use. They "say" it can be flush mounted to the wall - but NOT without a giant black brick below it. There are multiple photos in the ads of the TV "in use" but not a single one that shows that ugly black box!!! Here are my thoughts...
PRO... (and they are weak)
- A fairly good picture.
- Mediocre sound.
- The art option - which is also on the con - so it kinda wipes this one out. You chose a piece and it will stay on for up to 4 hours. There is a setting to adjust 1, 2, 3 or 4 hours.
- The best "pro"? The white frame was easily installed (it has magnets- but the little plastic pieces to secure the outer plastic to the frame are SUPER hard to secure. Good luck. I have provided a large number of photos to show all that I am outlining.
- It's a smart TV - which means you can hook up to your wifi and watch your netflix, prime, hulu, disney+.... but I will say I had to login my "samsung acct" in order to "load" my Amazon prime. Really? Just more ways for Samsung to follow you - you have to agree to them tracking/tracing you. GRRRR... I should move this to the con list... another pro/con that wipe each other out.
CONS....
- First and foremost - that UGLY black box. Approximately 9"x4"x1 1/2" . You cannot use the tv without it. The power cord plugs into it. If you planned on flush mounting (which is included with the TV - the most complicated and awful install imaginable) you will have an ugly black box under the TV.
- We had to purchase an adjustable frame to mount to the wall in order to hide the black box behind it. AND a white power cord so that the "showing" cord is at least white. I may hire an electrician to put a plug in behind it but at this point you have to wonder how much more I will spend to make this work as the photos all show. GRRRR
- The remote. Good luck getting the back open to put the batteries in!! It doesn't just "slide" open as the only direction on this is printed on the remote - and arrow pointing to the end of the remote. If you find yourself with one of these TVs - here's a hint... get a dime. Gently work into the top where the red plastic (the infrared tip) and the white body of the remote... wiggle it - ever so gently - back and forth... We eventually got it open. Sheesh.
- We attached the ugly black box to the back of the TV which means we had to install the pull away mount to have room to do that. So NO flush mount - which I was really looking forward to.
- The art.... very pretty. You get to see ONE - You MUST sign up, with a credit card, for a 31 day free trial to see any others. It also will not allow you add your own photos unless you sign up. It costs $4.99 a month after the trial. There are a lot of art options - but is it worth $4.99. I am on the fence. Because it doesn't "look" as I was lead to believe it would look like - a flush mounted frame.

- Overall, I am hugely disappointed. The ads are very, very misleading. You will find in the official description the mention of a "mini box"... which the black box clearly is not - "mini" in anyway.
Also, you should know that if you purchase an adjustable wall mounting kit, you will likely need to alter it to fit. We had to rig with TWO mounting sets to make it work - The arms were not long enough. We also tried a larger kit but it showed beyond the edges of the frame even though the mounting kit was meant for a 32" TV. Eh.
For those that are curious - this TV is manufactured in Mexico.
I would recommend looking for something else - unless you're cool with the ugly black box, a monthly fee for art and a lot of cord dangle. We did make the choice to keep it - for now. The thought of trying to repack it was overwhelming. And in all honesty, we had NO IDEA how much we were going to have to go through to make this work. If we could have seen into the future, we would have taken the 3 hours to repack and return it. Live and learn. I really hope our experience can help others avoid our mistake!

The concept of being able to see who is at your door is great, but the Ring Doorbell Pro is not great. When installing the product, the wire connectors would not accept and lock the wires, I had to purchase different wire connectors. For the first three days, I kept losing power to the doorbell. I would have to reinstall it, the wires won't stay connected tightly to the doorbell no matter how tightly the screws are. I had to put a large amount of electrical tape to keep the screws from loosening and power being lost.
After that the doorbell worked as it should for approximately 3 weeks, it then started getting knocked offline and needed to be reset continually. If it was my wi-connection it would make sense that my other gadgets would also be losing their wi-fi connection, but that wasn't the case. 3 weeks ago my video view feed was black, no audio no picture. I reinstalled the doorbell, but it was a black screen view. I would get the notice that someone was at the door, but I could view them. I contacted the Ring customer service. After several days they replied, had me run some wi-fi diagnostics and send them screen shots. They said I needed a Ring Pro Chime, because I needed a wi-fi extender. If it worked okay at the first, why all of a sudden would it not work now? No response was received back customer service. I have not received the Ring Pro Chime as I was told I would to correct the problem. I had an electrician check my power voltage where the doorbell is installed, he said I have the correct voltage according to their instructions. As of today my doorbell is dead, it doesn't rind, video doesn't even pull up any longer. This is not a good product and I would not recommend it to anyone. It has been a waste of time and money.

A friend of mine bought one of these to take video of his kids. I tried it. It works fine for what it is and takes decent video, and I can see why people may not want a full-blown camcorder, but in the market today it makes no sense. Do yourself a favor and just buy a plain old digital camera instead because almost every cheap digital camera can do what a Flip does except better and sometimes for less money too.

Take for example the Canon SD750, which does everything the Flip does and much more for just around $30 extra plus a few bucks for a larger memory card. It takes good VGA video exactly like a Flip, plays it back on a 3-inch color screen with sound (four times larger than the Flip's 1.5-inch screen) in four different speeds of slow-motion if you want, has a real 3X optical zoom and a 4X digital zoom (Flip is 2X digital zoom only), uses SD memory cards that can easily and cheaply be upgraded and changed (with Flip you're limited to 2GB only and then you have to offload, while a 8GB card costs around $12), and like the Flip it can also play back video directly from the camera through a TV.

BUT you can also record video in different resolutions, with effects such as B&W and sepia tones, at different frame rates from 15fps to high-speed 60fps, either in full automatic exposure or with manual tweaks to things like white balance, with stop shutter action where the camera will take one frame every one or two seconds and then play it back as a video, etc. Or you can just leave it in full auto mode in which case it takes less than three seconds from the time you turn it on to the time you start recording. It gets along with Windows just fine without any software all (it comes with software but you don't have to use it). And of course it takes fabulous 7.1 megapixel regular pictures with an enormous number of features.

I use the Canon SD750 as an example only because I'm familiar with it. But almost any digital camera will do what the Flip does and more, and many of them will do it for the same price or even less. So to me at least it makes no sense to get a Flip unless you're willing to spend more money for simplicity or only want it for the cute factor.

This thing looks great but sounds and works poorly. I did a lot of research before purchasing and I thought this was the player to get (I wouldn't touch Apple, especially since radio is important to me). It had everything I wanted plus 8 gigs of (expandable) memory. But after learning how to use it, loading it up with music, pics and videos, and trying it for two days I sent it back. Pros and cons:

PROS:

- Great (expandable) capacity at a great price. Comparable Samsung and Creative products don't come close to holding this much music, video, etc. There's a reason after all why memory is the number one selling point for MP3 players.
- Good screen. Not as nice as the Samsung T9 (which is amazing), but still pretty nice. Video and photos look good as long as you're looking from straight ahead.
- Good tactile control. I really like the scroll wheel, which makes it easy to quickly cycle through menus and hundreds of songs. With the Creative Zen V Plus and the Samsung T9 you're at the mercy of the joystick or button.
- FM radio that's recordable. This is important to me. I passed on the Creative because it doesn't record radio. I wouldn't even consider an iPod because it has no radio at all (!!!).
- User-replacable battery.
- User interface is fast. That's important. A big strike against the Samsung is that it takes 3-4 seconds just to skip to the next song. When it comes right down to it, usability is key.

CONS:

- FM reception is bad. I live in a large city with lots of powerful FM stations that come in clear as day on every radio I've ever used. But not with this thing. Listening to FM is like listening to someone crumple a plastic bag.
- Recording functions are lame. The FM record level is so low that even at full playback volume it's hard to hear the recording while on the train(which is OK because it just records lots of static anyway). The voice recording lacks sensitivity.
- Scratches easily. I was as careful as I could be with my new toy, and my first day taking it out of the house it still got 4 or 5 small scratches on the front before I even got to work in the morning. Those little scratches are clearly visible and distort the light. I can only imagine what it would look like after a few months.
- User interface is just adequate. Wanna make a playlist on the fly? Good luck, because you have to play each song first in order to add it to the list. Wanna cue up the next song while listening to something else? Good luck, because I couldn't find any way to do that very basic function (if it's there it's not readily apparent). There are plenty of other quirks. All in all, it looks cool but isn't that easy to use.
- The four outside buttons are a pain. Control wheel is great. Buttons around the control wheel? Not so great.
- It's not large, but it is larger than its competitors. The Samsung T9 is 1/2 inch shorter and about 35% thinner. The Creative Zen V Plus is thicker but also much shorter. The iPod nano is of course much, much thinner and lighter.
- Volume is lacking. Even with MP3s that I know have high volume, the e280 can sometimes require turning up the volume very high to get the sound you want.
- Editing MP3 tag information does no good once your files are loaded onto the machine.

So........overall I was disappointed and I thank Amazon for taking it back and refunding my money. The e280 is much better to talk about than to actually use. If FM and recording performance isn't important to you then you should add one star to this review.

And here's a tip if you do buy the e280 -- make sure the ID tag info on your MP3s is in order BEFORE you load up the machine. Because changing the tag info once the machine is loaded up won't make the album, artist and song menus any better. Do it first.

This GE BACKLIT UNIVERSAL REMOTE CONTROL (Backlit, 8-Device, Graphite, 47510) has terrific bright backlighting, and works with my Samsung TV, but has too many buttons! With my other remotes, you simply select the Input (Source), and all of the buttons will work to control the display, channels, etc. With the GE remote, you have to press a device/procedure button (e.g., TV, Stream) IN ADDITION TO selecting the Input/Source, or else the control buttons on the remote will NOT work properly.

I spent 12+ hours over several days on setup, testing, and investigation and cannot recommend this camera in its current state due mostly to setup difficulty. If I were not tenacious, I would have thrown this in the garbage and given up. I still have not gotten everything to work, but after reading the other reviews several times and Internet research, I was able to get almost everything working as I wanted it.

Once I got this working, the images were pretty good (but distorted) as long as the software was setup up to record in high definition. Below are the PROS and CONS and my experiences during setup.

PROS

- The camera is small and except for the lights, unnoticeable.

- It comes with mounting screws in case one wants to secure the metal base. However, double-stick tape is provided to mount the metal plate without using the screws. Since the camera base is magnetic, there may be no need to mount any plate as it can be placed on the fridge, pet playpen, or anything that is metal.

- Once the high definition is selected, the picture is pretty good even if slightly distorted. Any other setting except for high definition results in a grainy image.

- The camera stores the images on the SD card which is visible through the cloud. I used a [[ASIN:B013CP5IWO SanDisk Extreme 64GB MicroSDXC UHS-1 Card with Adapter (SDSQXNE-064G-GN6MA)]] in the camera.

CONS

- The camera is unusable unless cloud setup is done and the SD card is initialized. This means that besides a wireless network and SD card, a Smartphone or tablet is needed to download the EZVIZ app.

- The setup can be an absolute NIGHTMARE. For some people, things just work. However, for others like me, it takes lots of effort and guesswork to set up the software.

- No images are available in the cloud even after cloud setup. When I took the camera offline after hours worth of recording, I was not able to view any stored images. Therefore, the comment that there is cloud storage after setup appears to be untrue based on my results. When trying to play a video, I got the message "Video playback failed, error code:340405."

- Although I could remove the SD card from the camera and see a list of MP4 and PICT files on my computer, I was unable to view any of them. I tried on both Windows 10 and Windows 7 laptops without success. For the MP4 files, I tried Windows Media Player, IE, Audacity, Movie Maker, and QuickTime. With media player I got the error: "Windows Media Player cannot play the file. The Player might not support the file type or might not support the codec that was used to compress the file." With QuickTime (which is supposed to be able to read MP4 on a file open), I got an "Error -2048: Couldn't open the file hiv00084.mp4 because it is not a file that QuickTime understands." Since PICT is a Macintosh picture image, for those files I downloaded a trial version of Adobe Photoshop. When opening the PICT files, I got the error message "Adobe PhotoShop CC 2015. Could not complete the request because it is not the right kind of document." The files that get created on the SD card and which I should be able to open but cannot on a laptop are as follows:

hiv00000.mp4
hiv00000.pict
hiv00001.mp4
hiv00001.pict
....

- The images / videos taken are concave even in high-definition. It was as if I was looking through a drinking glass to view the images. I assume this may be typical of many cameras, but I cannot be sure. My dashcam images are not distorted like this. The first image I attached via a screen capture demonstrates this. This first image was not in high-definition, instead it was using the default resolution.

- The nighttime image is useless if the camera is facing glass (window, mirror, etc.) as you can see from the high-definition second image I attached. (PS Ignore the volume control bar as that accidentally came up when I was taking a screen shot with my other tablet.)

- The software is quirky. For example, besides not being intuitive, sometimes the software would not auto rotate on my tablet and other times it did.

- This camera is SUPER CREEPY. At night, when I turned off the IR light setting, the camera actually took a picture of the inside of my house even though I had it facing out toward my balcony. In certain situations, it must use the window as a reflector to capture the image behind it when the IR light setting is off. The image taken was very visible even though it was almost in X-Ray looking form. I was really "creeped out" by this. (The IR light setting says" When disabled, the image remains colorful with more image noise in dark environment." "When enabled, the image turns black and white with clear image in dark environment."}. What this is supposed to mean is the image in front of the camera; not behind it.

MY SETUP EXPERIENCE

Most people do not have to worry about this but since I have MAC address filtering security set on my router, I needed the MAC address of the camera for the router to allow the camera to connect. The MAC address is not in the documentation, but I accidentally found it when I dropped the camera and the camera cover came off. It is written on the main chip below the camera faceplate. Therefore, the steps I took for setup were:

- Added the MAC address of the camera into my router's MAC address filtering list.

- Inserted the 64GB micro SD card into the tiny slot on the side of the camera as per the instructions.

- Plugged in camera.

- Downloaded the EZVIZ app from Google Play (since I have an Android device) on my Google Nexus 7 tablet.

- Once installed, I opened the app. The screen displayed was nonsensical. There were stick drawings in the center and if I rolled my fingers from left to right it scrolled around the screen. I assume the app was designed for those who understand images with no words. Since I did not, I exited the app and and re-opened it. It was then that I got a different screen that enabled me to start to creating an account.

- Once I typed in my email address and password I wanted, I hit finish. The book does not detail what is supposed to be done. It assumes everyone knows. I got a message that said "Operation failed; failed to get the verification code. (99999)." After trying several times, I quit for the second day in a row. I even wrote the company but they never responded.

- The next day I tried again but this time I clicked on the check mark on the keyboard when I was done inputting my email and password and that worked.

- I attempted to add my camera after sign-in by clicking on the + sign as directed in the manual. It's at this point that I was asked to log into my network. Even though the network and password was correct, the login failed. I even disabled the MAC address filtering temporarily and tried again. Still no luck. I then wired this directly to the USB port on my router and it still failed with the message "Operation failed. Please try again. (102000)." I had enough and quit for the day.

- The next day, I re-read the reviews on Amazon. User Leslie mentioned in her review that "the specs for the camera say it works on a 2.4GHz band." She said that she set her "phone to only use the 2.4 band and not roam to the 5GHz band." That made me realize that I had to connect my Google Nexus 7 to the 2.4GHz band and not the 5GHz band. I mistakenly assumed that the camera was picking up my wireless network and trying to connect. It appears that it has to use the band of the phone or tablet to connect. Once I did this, I was able to add the camera by following the remaining directions in the book--scanning the QR code on the camera, etc. etc.

- I attempted to complete the rest of the instructions related to setup through device settings but that also was impossible to find. I eventually discovered that by tapping on the > sign next to my camera name (it's the > to the right that you can see in the first picture I attached), I would get to settings. I was looking for a gear icon but that's not how you get to settings in this software. Once I found the settings it was pretty easy to initialize the SD card, change the device password, etc.

- The next problem I had was actually seeing more than the image on the screen. In order to set up high definition, you have to click on the image itself. It's at this point that I was able to change the settings to full-screen mode, change from basic, standard, or HD images, take a picture, capture a recording, or turn the sound on or off.

In summary, I cannot recommend this camera due to the setup hassles, distorted video, inability to read the files on the SD card without the app, and the difficulty of navigating around the EZVIZ software. Also, the fact that changing one setting displays the contents of a person's house even if the camera is pointing toward a parking lot, is SUPER CREEPY. It also records conversations almost one room away. I unplugged mine and may only plug it in from time to time when I'm out of the house because this concerns me. Another thing to be wary of is the legal ramifications of recording voice and video; however, that applies to any recording or video capturing device and is not an issue specific to this camera.

I tried this speaker on the Google Nexus 7, iPhone 5, and iPad 3.

- With the Google Nexus 7 the speaker would only work very well while on Bluetooth connected to Rock Out (the speaker's Bluetooth). If I connected the cable to the headset port, the sound only came out as a whisper. I verified that the volume was on max on both the speaker and the Nexus 7. The documentation says "Know that when you're hardwired in for sound, the external controls are optimized for Apple devices." This explains why my Nexus 7 does not work when wired to the speaker.

- With the iPad 3, I was able to connect via the headset port and via Bluetooth without any problems and the sound was adequate but not fantastic even on the highest volume.

- With the iPhone 5, I was only able to connect via the headset port. When we connected via Bluetooth no sound would come out of the device. My boyfriend and I tried several times (about 6 times). We tried while on both the cellular network and also on my wi-fi network and were able to connect to Rock Out but never could get the sound to work. There was one time where it disconnected itself when we went back to look but except for that once, it remained connected throughout. There's a Bluetooth Memory reset by turning the speaker on, pressing and holding the power button for 10 seconds and then pairing the device with the iPhone. I verified that the unit was also fully charged. As long as I was connected via the headset cable I could answer calls by pressing the play button on the unit. However, no matter what my boyfriend and I did, we could not get Bluetooth to work on the iPhone 5.

The R0S2 is definitely rugged and when it works the sounds is adequate to very good. Only my boyfriend's iPhone 5 with the OtterBox installed would fit into the case of the unit for storage. Anything larger than this won't fit, which means the device has to be hanging off the unit if Bluetooth does not work or Bluetooth will have to be used so that the case can remain zippered up.

Based on my measurements, any item that is 5-1/2 inches wide by 2-3/4 inches tall by 1/2 inch thick should fit inside the case. I also weighed the case and it was almost one pound (15.7 ounces). For me it is not worth it to carry an extra pound of gear backpacking. Also, unless one is kayaking, biking, or out in the sun, the unit does not charge in the shade and according to the directions, it takes 8 hours to fully charge via solar power.

As long as there was some sun, I noticed the unit charging. As per the directions, it will take about 8 hours to solar charge. I charged mine in about 2 hours using my computer's USB port. The documentation says the run time is 10 hours but after almost two hours of use, I noticed only 2 bars on the charge when I plugged it back in for recharging.

The unit can be daisy chained to other Rock Out speakers for more sound. The unit has a 3.5 mm audio jack (line-level) and a 5V USB charging cord. According to the box, the speakers are 3W. The battery is a Lithium-ion, 3.7V, 800 mAh, 3Wh.

Another thing I noticed is that because the case bottom is not totally flat, the speaker has to be balanced to sit upright without falling over. Every time I tried it either fell forward or back so I had to lean it against something. Of course if it is secured to backpack or bicycle basket this is a non-issue.

In summary, I love the rugged case and think the sound is great to just okay depending on the item or material being played or the device it is paired with. I like that movies can be paused just by pressing the pause button on the speaker or that I can go to the next song by pressing the advance button. I have a hard time believing that backpackers will want to carry this almost one-pound speaker with them especially if hiking in the woods where there is usually no sun to charge the unit. Even though the bungee cord around the outside of the unit is thin, it has some clip hooks attached for fastening to a backpack or bicycle basket that should keep it secure. I like the olive green color because it is camouflaged for nature as it was designed to take backpacking. I give this 2.6 stars and recommend with reservations because the unit does not always work with the headset jack or on Bluetooth. Whether it is going to work or not apparently depends on the unit being connected to the device. When it works it's great; when it doesn't it is disappointing. I think the current price of $129.99 is also a bit steep.

These are only first impressions of this amp and I will update this review later if necessary. Marantz has actually replaced the 6004 with a newer model, the 6005 which has digital inputs but the 6004 continues to be readily available. It can be had now for about $200 less than its previous price and at $399 it's a real steal.

First let me address the assembled in China issue. Yes I would have preferred that it had been assembled in Japan, but its build quality seems excellent to me and I am basing my review upon my hands on impressions of the unit without prejudging it just because it was assembled in China.

It's rated at 45 WPC into 8 ohms which doesn't seem like much but it drives my less than efficient vintage ESS HD1500 speakers without missing a beat. Having the volume knob at 11:00 produces ear shattering volume with no noticeable distortion so I am quite pleased with its power. And remember that its power is rated with 0.08% THD which is an honest power rating. Other manufacturers may rate an amp at 100 WPC with 1% THD, but don't be fooled by that. 100 watts with 1% distortion is arguably less power than 45 watts with .08% distortion. I suspect that this amp will provide sufficient clean power for the vast majority of users.

Its sound is very mellow and laid back and lacks the harshness that some amps in this price range may be plagued with. I actually had to adjust the brilliance controls on my speakers back to a neutral position. I had them turned down to accommodate my old Onkyo amp. I have it connected to an inexpensive Pioneer CD player, my Directv satellite receiver, a bluray player and my PC via a Fiio E10 DAC and I have to say that it sounds excellent with any of those sources. I'm especially pleased with how it sounds with a good quality Internet radio stream such as some of the Soma FM stations. And with some of my audiophile quality Telarc CD's it totally blows my socks off. It produces good punchy dynamic range for classical music, and disco music with a heavy beat plays well with this amp too. I am using it in the source direct mode since I found no need to adjust its tone controls.

I do have one minor quibble but it's not enough to justify docking it one star. The only way to put the amp into standby mode is with its supplied remote control. The power button on the unit itself turns the unit completely on or off but won't put it into standby. And conversely the remote will only put it in standby and won't turn it completely off. So if you put it into standby with the remote and then try to turn it back on with the power button on the unit that won't work. So be sure you don't lose your remove. And the owner's manual doesn't explain this distinction very well.

But overall it's a great amp at a great price and i would heartily recommended it to any one looking for a good amp on a budget.

Edit - After 2 1/2 years of use the unit went dead on me. I tried to turn it on one morning and all I got was a flashing red LED on the front panel and that's it, no sound. I called Marantz support and was told I needed to send it away for repair. Thankfully its three year warranty was in effect.

What upsets me is that even though I had done nothing wrong and the unit was under warranty I had to pay to ship it to the repair shop. This is just wrong. Since the unit went bad under warranty shouldn't they have to pay for the shipping? I will never but another Marantz product again.

Anyway, they did pay for return shipping and I have it back and it seems to be OK now. But boxing it up and paying to ship it was an ordeal I should not have had to go through.

Let me start, we are a family of dedicated logitech-harmony remote users for the over 7 years. We love the easy of set up and allowing you to out in a large number of electrical devices onto one remote.

1. when using the harmony software there were a lot of limitations when compared with the 900 (and previous models). The limitations included:
a> couldnt change the order of the activities. ie if you want dvd ahead of music, you would not do that. To over come this: you need to preplan the order at which the devices are set up. In the more expensive models and in previous older models, you could set everything up and then re-order them.

The software is similar to other harmony remote, but once you indicate which remote you have: the choices are very limited.

It is worth buying the 900 and above for living room devices; and if you could find the 880, its former model, get it as the functionalities are much better. And yes, the software will support this older model. Buy the 700 if it is only for a couple of applicances. However, if you are a harmony user, you will feel a little frustrated with the limitations of this model.

I have always favored Verbatim products, particularly their CD-R Audio platters, so I was excited to try the Clip-It as a storage device. It does indeed work as advertised, but it is not a particularly remarkable product.

As a 4GB storage device, it does well enough but I noticed that the copy rate is somewhat slow. I did a side-by-side comparison with a SanDisk Cruzer stick and found that the SanDisk outperformed the Verbatim by an average of 2 meg/sec. That's an appreciable speed difference! When copying larger files, it means longer waits while the copy completes. For the impatient, this is bad.

I do not like the fact that the contact points are exposed and there is no cover for them. This equates to more opportunities for dirt and oil to contaminate the contacts which may eventually affect reliability.

As a paper clip (this product's other touted function) it performs well for a small number of pages but quickly is outdone when trying to clip together more pages or pages made with thicker paper.

I'm sorry, but I cannot recommend this product. There are other storage solutions that are comparable in price that perform better, have more storage space and are of better design.

The thing is, I have a wireless router upstairs on the same floor as the radio (Apple Time Capsule) and the wireless signal is quite strong. The other devices that connect to this router never have a problem with connectivity - devices that include a Roku box, a Chumby, my iPhone, my HP netbook, my Macbook, etc.

Sanyo DS25390 is a simple, no- frills television that offers enough features to get by but is lacking in some of the basics that we now take for granted in television sets, making it a questionable choice of sets for many consumers. Starting with the remote control, this television is very limited and quite out of date. Besides the usual keys (the ten numbered buttons, power button, etc.), you get a set- up key, CC key (closed captioning), Enter, and a Previous Channel selector. The various settings for the television can be accessed from the remote using the menu button, and they include the usual options (changing brightness, color, etc.). There isn't much more to it than that and the control itself has an old- fashioned look to it.

Picture quality on Sanyo DS25390 is okay, but nothing exceptional. The sharpness is the greatest weakness of this Sanyo television. Depending on your distance from the screen, the images seem a little fuzzy on the edges. At a good distance, this problem is minimized well enough that most people will not notice but it is definitely not as sharp as the picture on most newer models.

Picture quality is most important, but one other important consideration when choosing any television is its features and friendliness to accessories. Sanyo DS25390 has limited abilities and limited features. Chief among these is the limits on input. There are only a few input and output jacks and, because of this, there is no way to directly hook up a DVD player or video camera. This fact alone would probably discourage most people from considering this television. You could probably connect a DVD player or other device by going through a VCR first, but how many among is still own a VCR? I realize this television set was considered acceptable during its day, but it is difficult to overlook things like this.

One other problem I have with this television is the sound quality. There is only one small speaker, so the sound delivered is in mono. This certainly reduces the sound quality when watching certain movies or music video. The sound is acceptable for most television shows because the need for stereo quality isn't important. But it isn't very good for certain films and other programs that are greatly enhanced with stereo sound.

Overall, Sanyo Model DS25390 is a difficult television set to evaluate. It seems adequate in some ways and it was probably considered a good television set when it was first introduced. But compared to modern televisions, I cannot imagine anyone buying this set. The fact that a DVD player cannot be directly hooked up to this television is reason enough to reject it. Add to that the picture quality and its lack of sharpness and you have a television set that is too flawed to recommend. It's inexpensive, yes. But you most certainly get what you pay for.

I was on my third replacement Fire 10" tablet and the same issue started happening again. I wanted no part of a 4th replacement so I decided to get this Lenovo M10 Plus. One big selling point was in the Amazon description which stated "Throw in seamless Qualcomm Snapdragon octa-core processing. . ." Imagine my surprise on getting the tablet running CPU-Z and discovering it does not have a Qualcomm processor. CPU-Z reports a Cortex A-53, Lenovo's website says (as does the system information) that it has a Media Tek Helio P22T. This didn't make me happy. Trying to contact Lenovo made me even less happy.
But. . . I needed a tablet, I have a tablet, I'm going to keep it. Simple as that.
It does have a really sharp and clear screen. Color reproduction matches my laptop pretty well. I like the side firing stereo speakers. The remind me of my old Samsung 10" tablet that had speakers in the bezel that were aimed at your face. These are a close second. The Dolby Atmos controls take a while to tweak but sound reproduction is above average. I'm a little disappointed at how restrictive Lenovo is with Android 9. My settings menu, even with developer options turned on, I look like a strict business product that the corporation doesn't want the employees messing around in.
Performance is ok, this isn't a gaming rig and it shows. I tried Castle Wreck which I play on my Galaxy S9 phone and it ran, horribly, but it didn't crash. But again, I needed a tablet because I'm disabled and spend a lot of time flat on my back. I watch videos from several sources, surf the web and my casual games, cribbage, backgammon, etc. run fine.
I had to get a case for it. The tablet screen is slightly bigger 10.3" vs my old Fire's 10.1" but the tablet itself is significantly smaller than the Fire. It's thinner, lighter and the bezels are almost non-existent. That, plus the incredibly slick aluminum back made holding the tablet while laying down difficult to say the least. Found an affordable 3rd party cover that does what I needed.
All in all? The screen is stunning. It runs everything I need it to though not all I wish it would. Price was right and it had a full year warranty. It'll do.

I have had several water resistant shower speakers and none, not one, my $600 Samsung Galaxy phone isn't. . . nothing is waterPROOF. It's a lie. Many advertisers and sellers like to claim waterproof status but what they mean is water RESISTANT. IPX7 means a device can survive immersion, up to 1 meter (3 ft 3 in) depth for up to 30 minutes. Let's also be clear here; those tests were with pure, likely purified, filtered water not highly chlorinated pool water. Not salty sea water. Not brackish lake/pond/river water. And also not water containing soaps, shampoos and conditioners. All that. . . stuff in every day water is going to reduce the effectiveness of the water resistance of any device.
So, I unbox this and it's light. Lighter than just about any speaker I've used. I look at the specs. . . 3 watts. THREE watts of power? Okay it's supposed to be primarily used in a small enclosed indoor space but it also says it's great for camping, hiking and general outdoors stuff (please, don't blast music when you're hiking, wear headphones, show some respect and restraint). I've never seen a non-novelty speaker that was less than 5 watts. It feels light and cheap and thin. The suction cups; they send two likely expecting one to fail. Neither worked. The best I could get with the cup wet with soapy water, alone, no speaker, stuck to a mirror for maybe five minutes. I can't get these suction cups to stick to my desk. No worries, my shower has a shelf. I turned off my oontz Angle 3 and connected this to my phone using Samsung Music as a player to take advantage of the Dolby Atmos and excellent sound (only PowerAmp sounded better of the half dozen players I tested and PowerAmp is a paid app only) quality it offers. I guess if you wanted noise in the shower this would work. Sound quality was about as bad as you'd expect. Distorted bass, harsh highs, muddy midrange. No EQ settings I tried made this sound good. It's just not worth it. You can for just a little more money get far better sounding water resistant speakers. You should enjoy the music in your shower or bath not suffer with it.

A seller replaced a different defective FM transmitter unit with this one for me (mine has the Kollea brand name on it, but this is the identical unit, private-labeled). This is a better product than what it replaced, but is not without it's flaws. I have three (*UPDATE: now four, and the fourth one is a deal-breaker--see below) complaints with this unit:

1) It will not automatically reconnect to my phone about 75% of the time. I have to manually shut Bluetooth off and turn it back on on the phone, sometimes a few times before it pairs successfully. This is a hassle--a PITA. Every time I get in the car, I have to go through this process--every time power is cut from the transmitter, actually, so if your passenger knocks it and it pops out of the 12V socket, it will have to be re-paired, which is supposed to happen automatically, but does not, and you then have to go through the process. Frustrating.

2) Charge output is only 1.0A. this is why I returned the first one--phone gives a "slow charging" warning when charging from this unit, regardless of what USB cable I use (I tried four different cables, all of which I know for certain can carry 2.1A).

3) Callers have occasionally complained they cannot hear me well when using this unit, and I occasionally (but not often) encounter FM interference. I believe Bluetooth itself is part of the problem, and anyone who has used a few Bluetooth headsets or units like this knows audio quality is terrible. Period. We just deal with it. Add to that the burden of having to transmit your signal via FM to a car stereo and the user-side audio (what you will hear in your car) is always going to be craptastic.

4) (*UPDATE) When paired, voice recognition on my phone, which is usually quite good, becomes severely impaired. This is also likely the culprit for complaint #3, above. I suspect this is because when paired, it tries to use the built-in microphone for voice recognition instead of the microphones on my phone (of which there are 4). It is disabling the extremely good microphones in my phone (Nokia lumia Icon which is well known for having incredible audio input) and using the unit's crappy microphone instead. This microphone is located in the unit, which is attached to the center console of my car near the shifter, and thus picks up all the vibrations and related road and engine noise transmitted through the structure of the car as I drive. This approach is terrible. I have stopped using the unit for anything requiring voice input, including telephone calls. In other words, this is just a big awkward charger now, and one that charges painfully slowly (see complaint #2). If it were possible to disable the onboard mic, and use the mics in my phone instead for calls and voice recognition, this would be a much more serviceable unit As it is now, it is just a piece of junk.

Cannot recommend this item. There are definitely worse products out there. I have not tried them all, but of those I have used, this is the best one so far. I will likely keep using it until the lack of automatic pairing pushes me over the edge with it one day and I get something else. (*UPDATE: this thing just does not work well, and I am now looking for something else.)

I replaced it with the [[ASIN:B012F0DGYE Sony ICFP26 Portable AM/FM Radio (Black)]], which performs a lot better and costs about $3 more. If you're looking for an "el-cheapo" digital frame, you may have hit the jackpot with this one. Not only is it relatively low-priced, but it also comes with low quality picture reproduction, low quality sound, and badly thought out button placement.

To be fair, it takes flash drives and camera cards, and plays MP3s and videos and can do slideshows and tell you the time and date.

But...

The power cord makes the whole "hanging on the wall" thing a bit of a joke, the lack of internal memory is a pain I'd rather not have, and the music that comes out of the in-frame speakers certainly isn't the food of love.

The USB cord mentioned in the booklet is not included, so if you don't happen to have one handy you'll have to use flash drives and camera cards for picture storage.

Talking about photographs, this frame will take your 3MB memories and make them look like 70KB internet snapshots, so this may not be a good gift for your favorite photo-take-outerer.

Navigation is tricky and could be a lot easier, and the buttons and doo-dads are awkward to negotiate, especially as the button color blends in with the back of the frame.

I guess you could give this to your dear old Gran, especially if she has failing eyesight and hearing, and you were able to visit her daily to set it up and change the pictures, but in this high-tech world, anyone else would expect much better picture and sound quality.

Economically priced, and not worth the price tag.

Amanda Richards, June 6, 2009

We've had trouble with the remote for three months now. It works sporadically at best and has finally died entirely. This is a major problem because you cannot do important stuff with the sound bar without the original remote control. Such as.... rebooting it. If you change your WiFi network like.... getting a new router, then you cannot simply go to the app and update the connection. You must reboot the entire sound bar via the remote control only. WHICH DOES NOT WORK AT ALL. This design flaw has rendered the entire sound bar none functional because it cannot connect to the new Wi-Fi - going back to our old router isn't an option because it died. So now I have a sound bar that technically is operational, yet cannot be used. Our Bose 500 sound bar was able to be reconfigured for the Wi-Fi swap because it's remote works like a champ - it's also significantly simpler in design than the 700 remote. (I'll end up spending fifty bucks for a new 700 remote and that really aggravates me)

******* Original review before the drama*******

We've had an older Bose Solo 15 Series II TV Sound System in our living room for a couple of years and we've been pretty happy overall. I recently put the Bose 500 version of this sound bar in our master bedroom and was amazed at the difference, so getting this 700 for the living room was a no brainer. I mostly just expected them to connect as a group and have the same sound, but this 700 is better than the 500.

It's a long, narrow, sleek looking unit with glass finishes that makes it almost invisible in front of the Tv. Our Roku fits alongside without drama. The connections are via digital optical cable or the HDMI. Just turn off your TV speakers - not mute, off from the tv settings. You need to use the included wired headset to fully set the speakers for your room's accoustics. I'm using this bar with a 55", 3 years old, Sceptre dumb tv and a Room streaming stick - the connection was immediate and drama free.

You must use the Bose app to get full functionality out of the sound bar. The app let's you connect two or more Bose speakers with the tech and use them all simultaneously as a group to play music or audiobooks etc. The app also starts the set up for the Alexa link and the streaming services like Prime, Tune In, Bluetooth streaming and others. You can also set 6 favorites as one touch launch options.

Alexa works fine through the sound bar, but the response speed is noticably slower than through a regular Echo. I get a glitchy message saying "This unit is unable to perform routines" every time I say "Good morning". Good morning triggers a specific set of actions from Alexa to turn on our bedside lamps, the bathroom lights, turn off our porch lights, give me the weather and then our daily news brief. Despite that glitchy message, every morning, the Bose performs our routine flawlessly. It's weird, but not a big deal really.

The sound quality is excellent and immersive in multiple settings from music to a movie. The app let's you adjust the sound quality and balance with bass, treble and center. You can also set it for dialogue mode to enhance/clarify voices and reduce background noise - this is very handy for the news or a talk show. Take some time to adjust the settings for what your ear really likes and you'll be amazed at the fullness of sound and all the background details.

After two weeks, I'm incredibly pleased with the build quality, looks, sound and full functionality of both the 500 and 700 units. The 700 wins out by a nose over the 500 for us because the sound is bigger, but mostly because the remote control is better. The remote lights up when you lift it and you can find the buttons instantly. I programmed our TV to the Bose remote and it controls the sound bar, channels up and down and power for both the tv and the sound bar. Bottom line is that I am now looking at buying another 700 for the master bedroom and moving the 500 to our guest suite so we'll have the full set.

I wasn't expecting much given the price of this item, and I got pretty much what I expected.

The charging port is hard to reach and the LED charging indicator is difficult, if not impossible to see, without having to move the foam earpiece covering.

Setting up/pairing the device is pretty easy. Press the button for 4 seconds or so and you’ll hear a pleasant female voice say, “Hello”. This means the power is on. Continue holding the button and the device will enter pairing mode. You’ll hear the voice say, “Ready to pair.” When pairing is complete, you’ll hear the device say, “You’re connected” and tell you how much charge the battery has. So far, all I’ve heard is, “Battery full.” I have no idea what other battery indications the voice will give – perhaps only at 3/4, 1/2 and 1/4? Or maybe percentages?

The buttons are the biggest drawback with this device. Actually, it's really just one multi-function button on the right earpiece. The button functionality is not like any Bluetooth headset I've used before - very non-intuitive. The button has no label at all and the tactile feedback is nonexistent at times - I press the button sometimes and there's no "click" feeling. If a song is playing, it doesn't seem to matter where I press, the song stops if it is playing. When I press again, anywhere, it starts playing again.

There is no volume control on the headphones at all. You’ll have to adjust the volume from your phone/audio player. There is a bare bones EQ function. You control this by clicking the multi-function button 3 times in rapid succession. Each time you do this, the device advances to the next of 3 EQ setting – balanced, bass boost and JLab signature. The “balanced” setting seems to sound just like what it’s named – balanced or equal high, mid and low tones. The bass boos is decent – not overbearing. Not sure what the last one is, but if the pictograms in the manual are any indication, it boost the high and low ends. The EQ function does provide audible feedback – the voice announces each setting by name.

There's a next track function, but no function for going to the previous track. The next track function requires holding down the multi-function button for 2 seconds. There's no audible feedback for this function (other than a very short moment of silence). When you hear the silence, let go IMMEDIATELY. If you hold the button down for too long the Bluetooth connection will be severed and you'll have to reconnect.

Apparently, there's no ability to fast forward or rewind within a song or audio book. You'll have to do this on your phone/audio player. Pretty poor design if you ask me. BTW – I use this only with my audio player, so I did not test the phone/mic functions, but I’d be surprised if they were robust.

The instructions are minimal at best. The manual is one piece of paper printed on 2 sides. Unfolded, it's about the size of 2 business cards - about 4"x4.5" (10.16cm x 11.43cm). One side has instructions and the other is all promotions/disclaimers, etc. That's it.

Sound quality is acceptable - decent bass and stereo separation is good. I’m no audiophile though. The product description says it has "Noise Isolation", which is marketing speak used by all on-ear headphone manufacturers. It simply means the ambient noise is slightly reduced because the headphones cover your ears. Bottom line - there's no tech/function in this device that does any active noise cancellation.

The headphones are a little snug/tight, but not so much to be uncomfortable - at least that's my opinion after an hour+ of testing. Not sure if this will be true for something like a 3-4 hour flight. I’ll test this out in the near future and will update this review, if possible.

The charging cable that comes with the item is 9” long (22.86cm). Not very useful at all, but better than nothing.

On the plus side, the manufacturer did provide an extra set of foam earpiece covers - the set that comes on the headphones is orange. The extra set is black.

Bottom line, for $15 I wasn't expecting a lot - well maybe better button functionality, but hey, what can you do? As my granddad used to say, “You pays your money and you takes your chances.”

OK, take 2. My original review of this product got hijacked somehow. After writing it, I checked back a couple hours later and my screen name and original title were there, but my review got replaced with what seemed like some guy's journal entry. It had absoluterly nothing to do with this or any other product. Strange.

Anyway - as mentioned in my original posting, this review is more a condemnation or earbud headphones in general than the Sennheiser CX300-B, which I decided to try after my "over ear" style Sony noise canceling headphones went on the fritz. My past experience with earbuds was not good, although I had only ever tried the type that come with the iPod and not the "ear plug" type that go in the ear canal, like the Sennheiser CX300-B. However, having owned a pair of Sennheiser over the ear headphones back in the 70's, my impression of the company and their products was good. So, I decided to take the plunge. What a mistake.

After opening the package (no easy feat - damn sound welded plastic clamshells!), I popped on the medium-sized bud covers (appropriate for my size ears) and inserted them into my ears. I turned on my mp3 player and listened for a few minutes. The sound was adequate - nothing spectacular. I did notice they had decent bass and did block some external noise. I kept listening as I stepped outside to go to the store. I couldn't believe what I heard. Every step I took was amplified in my head - like a booming bass drum. Even the gentle bumping of the cord against my chest was amplified - a constant thump, thump, thump that was impossible to ignore. As it turns out, the very feature that blocks a modicum of external noise, also amplifies any sound that travels through the body. Even breathing is amplified! As I walked, it sounded as though I was listening to someone breathe over a PA system! I had hoped to use these while running, but there's no way that's going to happen. In fact, the problem with amplified sound is so bad, I won't use them at all.

I am very disappointed in this product and will never buy any ear plug style headphones again. I don't understand why anyone would sell them, let alone use them. They may have great sound reproduction, but the listening experience is totally ruined by the sounds that get amplified through the body. It amazes me that people buy similar style products that sell for hundreds of dollars. The only way you can enjoy the sound they produce is to sit perfectly still. I'm glad I only paid about $16 for these things. I won't return them because it'll be too much of a hassle - probably cost more to ship them back than I paid.

BTW - The photo of the product is misleading. The cord looks thicker than it actually is and there's no way it can be coiled as is shown in the photo. It gives the impression the cord is more supple and flexible that it really is. Also, one end of the cord is longer than the other. Not sure why this is, but the thinness of the cord makes it prone to kinking and tangling. In fact, since one side of the cord is longer than the other, it makes it even more prone to tangling.

Bottom line - steer clear of the Sennheiser CX300-B and all ear plug style earbuds.

There are many, many true wireless earbuds out there. What attracted me to these were the features that they boasted: Wireless Charging, Active Noise-Cancelling, and bluetooth 5.1. So how does these earbuds compare to some of the cheaper offerings and does it justify being twice as expensive as some of them?

In terms of price, these earbuds can be considered cheap. Comparable to the mid-tier brands out there such as Anker and MPow, and much, much cheaper than Bose and Jabra brands. Still, there are many that cost half the price.

With the pricing in mind, let's look at the good of these earbuds:
+ Long battery life -- I'm on my fourth hour of listening to an audiobook and the battery is still showing 50% on my phone.
+ Battery status reporting to phone -- I'm sure most of the recent bluetooth headphones and earbuds do this now, but it is still nice.
+ Type-C port for charging -- The move to type-c as the standard charging port for all devices is happening and I'm glad NANNIO didn't cheap out and use a micro-usb. One less cable to worry about.
+ No app necessary -- The passthrough and ANC features can be turned on by tapping the touch controls twice.
+ Google Assistant Support -- Tap three times and Google Assistant launches.
+ No ugly microphone stick -- The tear-drop shape of these buds look much better than the ugly sticks that Apple's products have, in my opinion.
+ Smooth transition between left-only, right-only, and stereo -- These earbuds allow one to choose to use only one earbud while keeping the other in the charger without having to pair the other piece separately. It's something that I take advantage of on long drives. I keep one bud in the ear to listen to my audiobook and switch out when the battery runs out.

The bad:
- Not low profile -- The Anker SoundCores is pretty inconspicuous in the ear, but these NANNIOs, being white and sticking out more are anything but low profile.
- ANC not very effective -- The ANC levels are adjusted to be pretty minimal on these buds so while it is possible to hear the difference between the feature being on and off, it is also noticeable that only the lowest hums are cancelled out. Earbuds simply aren't good for ANC. Buds simply don't fit perfectly in the ear canal and when the jaw moves, the fit shifts. By this fact, there is always sound leaking through, reducing the efficiency of any ANC system. In earbuds, ANC is really just a gimmick.
- Passthrough needs to have wind noise reduction -- The reason for passthrough, in my mind, is to be able to hear surrounding sounds if wearing earbuds while running. It uses the microphone on the earbuds to pass external sounds through, but when running, there will always be wind noise. Without wind noise reduction, it makes this feature useless. I don't know of any earbuds that have addressed this issue.

I thought I wouldn’t be picky when it comes to buying a new alarm clock; I mean, I owned a Sony Dream Machine (yeah, you too?) for over 30 years and that had minimal features! At least, that’s what I thought until I actually started looking for a new one.

When you look at the possibilities out there you start to think that perhaps I need:
- Bluetooth? It would be nice to wake up to a playlist I set up in my phone.
- Good sound quality? If I’m gonna have bluetooth, the sound quality needs to be good.
- Projection? It would be nice to see the time on the ceiling with the press of a button.
- Atomic? It would be nice to NOT have to manually set the time for Daylight Savings.
- Temperature/Weather? It would be great to know the weather when I look at the time -- especially if it is projected on the ceiling!

The Soundbot tries to provide many of these features but fail to put them together into one cohesive unit. It tries to be an alarm clock and bluetooth speakers but fails at both.

The Good:
- Great looking design. The wood look and the size, color and placement of time and temperature all add to a great look for the Soundbot.
- Impressive sound. As I’m currently searching for a bluetooth portable speaker (and have already reviewed a few), I pay special attention to sound quality. It’s comparable to the Jambox Mini.
- Touch controls. No buttons to detract from the wood look of the clock. The snooze, volume, and phone buttons are all touch sensitive.
- Time is remembered even when unplugged.

The Bad:
- The clock does NOT play a bluetooth when the alarm goes off. The workaround is to use your phone as the alarm, but what’s the point?
- No Next/Prev track buttons. The +/- buttons only control volume.
- Only one level of dimming. You can choose full or half brightness with the snooze button but it is still a little bright for me. I have to turn the clock away while I sleep.
- Alarm only has one sound: an annoying beep.

Tip:
The alarm clock can be set to go off every day (the alarm LED is solid, not flashing). When the alarm goes off, PRESS and HOLD any touch-sensitive button to disable the alarm for today. It will then go off again tomorrow.

Conclusion:
With the inability to use the bluetooth as an alarm tone, and without an FM Radio as an alternative, the Soundbot serves as a pretty poor alarm clock. You’re stuck with a simple beep. Without a next/prev track button, the Soundbot serves as a pretty poor wireless speaker. The good sound quality is the only thing it has going for it.

I have had the opportunity to review many headsets and headphones over the years and without question the recent technological advancements have aided this area by leaps and bounds.

Since the earbuds can be used together for stereo sound or individually you can potentially double play time by using one at a time. Even with this, 3 hours of playtime from wireless earbuds is way below average. Even having the case which allows charging on the go, this doesn’t mitigate the frustration of having to charge after a few hours of listening.

The charging case is cool. It allows for Qi charging of devices and will act as a portable power supply. The downside to this is the size and weight. Sometimes I want to travel light and this set does not allow for that.

After receiving, I made sure the case was fully charged then confirmed each earbud had a full charge. After verifying full power within each earbud I followed the simple pairing instructions and had no problems whatsoever. Once the earbuds are removed from the case they first pair with each other then you simply pair with your Bluetooth device.

These earbuds will require testing which of the 4 sizes of ear bud caps work best for the individual user. I typically use the medium size which with this set the medium small ones worked better for me. I purchase sets of replacement memory foam ear bud pads which I ended up replacing them with as they are more comfortable and simply work better. The sound from these headphones is mediocre - from the bass notes to the midtones to the treble - not terrible but also not great. I tested these headphones with a wide range of audio - from audiobooks to jazz, heavy metal, country, classical and blues - everything just sounded ok.

I have listened to both music and audiobooks through these as I moved throughout my home and interestingly while these claim to be Bluetooth 5.0 they do not have near the range of other Bluetooth 5.0 sets I’ve tested. I estimate the effective range at around 20 feet.

While these are ok for listening to music, how are they for calling? The sound through these headphones is again mediocre- on both ends.

Controls are overly complicated and the buds do not always respond to the commands given which is especially frustrating when listening to an audiobook as I often skip ahead or back not intending too.

Being both an audiophile and a lover of all new tech when I first read about this technology coming out a few years ago I started looking forward to testing it.

So what are the potential advantages of bone conduction earphones? I’m glad you asked. When properly adjusted they allow the user to enjoy listening to whatever they choose while not blocking external noises, thus allowing the user to react to ambient noises. This should make them safe to use while driving or doing other activities that require hearing ambient noise in order to conduct safely.

As with other bone conduction headphones, these 9 Digital headphones allow for little fine adjustment. In order for this type of headphones to work properly and provide the highest sound quality they should rest flat, or almost flat against the skin between the front of the ear and the rear part of the cheek bone. When adjusting the speaker it will be clear when the speaker is properly adjusted. This set of headphones is designed to fall lower on the back of the head which for me pulled the speakers out of the ideal placement. While I have worked on adjusting this, it really is not possible. Due to this, sound quality is decent yet not optimal and surrounding people are able to hear what the listener is playing.

Just so it is understood, these headphones are rated IP53, meaning that they’re protected against dust, in so much as their inner workings won’t be compromised if dust were to get inside. They’re also protected against spraying water, with no pressure when tilted up to a 60-degree angle. This is a lower rating as compared to other headphones in this price range.

In terms of operation these headphones struggle to maintain a solid connection for anywhere close to the full 33 feet they are rated - typically Bluetooth 5.0 holds a connection with no problem though I have found that isn’t the case with these headphones. The batteries lasted approximately the amount of time listed. Sound quality is middle of the road especially due to not allowing for fine adjusting of the speakers.

This is a great technology with a lot of potential. I have tested and reviewed bone conduction headphones since they first were released a few years ago, due to how these fit and the connectivity issues this is not a set I would recommend.

For many years I have researched, written about and reviewed all types of security equipment - from the most advanced to the most simple. This set falls into the later category.

I have tested and reviewed several similar sets. Each of these sensors work based on a simple magnetic principle which is why it is critical they be mounted on the same plains, directly next to to each other when the door or window is closed. When open the magnet is released and the switch triggers causing the alarm to sound. This technology has been used with great success for many years.

The alarms are very loud and work the way they should. If the batteries lasted as long as the listing claimed this would be a reasonable set though they do not. These sets will require battery changes every 2.5-3 months, each sensor requires 3 AG13 or LR44 button style batteries. If all 6 sensors are utilized you will need 18 batteries every 3 months or 72 batteries a year. Not only does this get expensive but it is a hassle staying on top of the batteries always dying.

For those interested in utilizing these sensors, I recommend the following batteries: Eunicell SR44W 303 357 Silver Oxide Button Cell 1.55V Battery Long Shelf Life 0% Mercury (https://www.amazon.com/dp/B07MMTG4ZF/ref=cm_sw_em_r_mt_dp_7RB98F39642K4BXJ2Q2C) - while these are the same size and voltage they are made with better components and tend to last a bit longer and are far more consistent upon arrival.

After using these for 8 months I can say while these work and consistently sound when the sensors are separated there are far better options that use much more sophisticated, long lasting batteries. This is the type of product where you want a quality lithium ion battery that you can count on for many months or a year at a time - and ideally recharge it at that point.

After thoroughly testing this set I suggest looking into more sophisticated, sets that will cost slightly mor upfront but cost far less in the long run.

I have been working with security camera products for over 20 years - over that time I have installed systems for businesses, corporations and individuals - from enormous multimillion dollar systems to single camera nursery monitors. I’ve consulted on large projects and written about security vulnerabilities within networks for trade publications.

This is a field I know well. Over the years the technology has improved and become less and less expensive to produce. It is now practical to install security systems that would have only previously been used in commercial settings in residential. Unfortunately while the hardware has improved dramatically the software often has not - which is the case with this set.

The set I got did not come with a hard drive which wasn’t a big deal as I always have a few around. A suitable SATA Hard Drive can be purchased for $25-$400 depending on size and quality.

In terms of this system it should be clear based on the price - this is a budget system. That doesn’t mean it won’t work but these cameras are not going to pan, tilt or zoom (the lens is fixed).

If these are installed with this in mind they can still be very effective they just need to be positioned correctly.

For instance if these cameras were placed up high on a second floor overhang you would see an overview of the surrounding area but would not be able to zoom in to see facial characteristics. On the other hand, if placed on a porch a bit above head height you will have no issue making out the same. Placement is key.

In terms of wiring any POE (Power Over Ethernet) camera is excellent. The cameras are powered and transmit data over the same Ethernet cable. There are several advantages to these systems the most important is security as the cameras are not broadcasting wirelessly making them more difficult to hack.

The camera operation is excellent for the price. The images are clear and crisp and night vision operates without issue.

Where this set falls apart is on the software side - unfortunately this is often the case. The software is so non user friendly that it is almost unusable. I have used countless similar systems and this has to be among the all time worst software operating systems I have ever encountered.

There are countless glitches and bizarre, nonsensical methods for how it has to be initiated that it became comical as I worked through them all. I had been anxiously waiting to try out the NETGEAR Nighthawk. I’d read over the impressive specs long before it was released, I’ve read glowing reviews touting it as the fastest, most powerful router Netgear had yet to produce... Specially made for the high demands of Smart Homes. All the hype made it sound like it was going to be AMAZING.

Now that I’ve set it up and run a full battery of tests - honestly the best thing I can say about it is it looks cool. 😕

I have been working with NETGEAR products for 25+ years so setup was not a big deal. As with most of NETGEAR’s new products don’t expect much printed material - that’s OK with me... I downloaded the Nighthawk app and followed the directions - they are fairly straightforward.

Restart your modem, plug in your Nighthawk Router, plug Ethernet Cable from modem to router, connect cell to router’s network using the ID and password provided on the sticker on top of the routers plastic cover, return to app. Here is where things began making less sense.

When I return to the Nighthawk app it goes through the process of connecting to my router and I receive an error message: ROUTER NOT SUPPORTED. Odd, but I’ve learned when installing a new router anything can happen. I exit the app and return, same message. I exit the app, restart the router, wait and restart the app and it recognizes. Great - I’m in... no big deal.

I update the Firmware, change the network name and password and start checking through the settings. I notice right away there are very few settings within the app - no security settings tab, no parental controls tab - odd, but I’ve learned NETGEAR tends to move these types of things around when they redesign their apps, so I put that concern to the side.

I plug my Ethernet cables into the 1G ports (there are 4 of them) in the back and watch the lights on front illuminate.

One of these runs to my computer and once it initialized the internet connection I ran a speed test - I’d tested with my previous router just prior to switch and was consistently benching at 210Mb/s download and 15Mb/s upload. With the Nighthawk I speed tested at 130Mb/s and 9Mb/s - definitely not what I’d hoped to see but I knew all my smart devices were working on rejoining the network so that could be slowing it down.

I decided to give it some time to let everything register on the network. In the Nighthawk app I had 42 devices and about half were still listed as unknown.

I let it work for about an hour and it recognized the majority of them... I ran another speed test - again through my laptop connected via Ethernet through the Nighthawk and this time received 154Mb/s and 11Mb/s. Still not great.

Then I went into my Nighthawk app as it has a speed test feature in there - I try that and receive an error that I must be on the network to run a speed test. I was on the network. I exit the app and go back in and receive the message ROUTER NOT SUPPORTED again. Ugh - really???

I reboot the router again and then the app recognizes it. While I’m able to control the router the speed test function does not want to work. Not a huge issue. I went through the browser on my phone and ran a speed test. The results were absolutely pathetic. This is the NIGHTHAWK - the router that is supposed to provide blazing fast speeds to WiFi devices and I received results of 5.4Mb/s download and 2.1Mb/s upload - and similar on 3 consecutive tests. At this point I’m starting to be less than impressed.

I decided to log in to the more advanced router settings via my computer. I had no problem getting in there but to my surprise there are ABSOLUTELY NO PARENTAL CONTROLS. This is the same company that has sold itself as allowing you to have complete control over every aspect of your home internet. NETGEAR Genie is no longer available and the NETGEAR Nighthawk panel doesn’t even have a section for parental controls - let alone work with Disney Circle.

While there are some advanced security features available within the NETGEAR Nighthawk Router controls on the computer they are anything but user friendly - they are hard to find, hard to set, and less than optimal.

As I was discovering all of this and researching these issues in the NETGEAR Community Forums I started receiving notifications from my smart devices that they were losing WiFi signal and then after a minute or two they would reconnect. This happened with my security cameras, LIFX lights, Wemo switches, and August door locks. After this went on for about an hour I decided my experiment with the NETGEAR NIGHTHAWK had reached its conclusion.

Unfortunately I can’t recommend this router at this time. While the hardware inside should have this out performing most any other router on the market I found it to be slow and glitchy.
