[[VIDEOID:8bed6d79d90a43dd042702aefe52b20a]] I wanted to love this phone so badly. Now that LG has left the phone market, I wanted to know there are still flagship killers like Oneplus out there to take on the bullies of wireless phones. And on paper, there's a LOT to love about this phone. Let's mention the good things first:
- As a photographer, I really like the Hasselblad cameras that include a very capable manual mode. See the included photos taken with the phone, no fake bokeh effects. That's just the natural blurring DOF of the lens and sensor.
- As someone who is picky about user experience I absolutely LOVE the silent/vibrate/ring physical switch. All smartphones need that, in my opinion.
- CPU/GPU benchmarks are awesome, right up there with flagships that cost more.
- Coming from the Galaxy S10's terrible in-screen fingerprint reader, this one renews my faith in fp readers.
- Display is beautiful and crisp.
- Battery is surprisingly good.

In a nutshell, the hardware is great! If they just throw a stock Android OS on here, it would be perfect! But sadly, no... they didn't. And the software is TERRIBLE. Chock full of bugs.
Some examples (some of which I tried to capture on video):
1) Google Voice call redirects are broken.
I've been using GV as my phone number for nearly a decade and never had a single problem like this before. The stock dialer does not care what you set GV to, it will IGNORE your outgoing call redirect requests. No matter what you set it to, it uses the carrier number to call out. Even if you select "ask before each call", the phone is so excited to dial out it will show you the option to pick, but in the background IT STARTED CALLING ALREADY and clearly doesn't care what you want. To be fair, this started with the Android 12 update on the Oneplus 9 series as well, so it's a Oneplus problem in general, it seems.

2) Android Auto pop ups make no sense.
When you plug the phone into a USB port, it will prompt you with three options. Charge, Transfer Files / Android Auto, and Transfer Photos. When I plugged it into my car with AA, I see it starting on my car's display, but the pop up still appears on the phone. Naturally, I picked option 2, since it says android auto. It disconnects. So I unplug and try again, and leave it on charge, which seems to work. For the sake of testing, I also tried transfer photos, and it also worked. It seems that THE ONLY OPTION THAT DOESN'T WORK is the one that says Android Auto on it! Seriously?! Is it opposite day?! But that's ok, my car radio also supports wireless Android Auto (uses Wifi direct instead of a cable), so that should avoid the problem right?

3) Wireless Android Auto breaks Wifi's ability to reconnect to known networks.
I know what you're thinking... come on, right? How many Google features can Oneplus break at a time. Apparently a lot. When using Android Auto over the wireless connection, it actually works great, but then the phone seems to give up ever wanting to connect to my known wifi networks again. I get to work or return home and found out that I've been using cellular data the entire time, unless I manually go into Wifi settings and click join network. If I leave the coverage area or toggle wifi off/on, it won't reconnect. I have to manually connect it in settings each time or be stuck using my data plan. A reboot fixes the problem and the wifi reconnects as expected afterwards... until the next time I take the car somewhere and the problem comes back.

4) The 3.3x Telephoto camera has its own color science.
It doesn't match the others. The main camera is actually quite good, and the wide is decent as well. The telephoto is a bit less vibrant and noticeably more dull on warm color themes. I though these were Hasselblad tuned and calibrated to have professional color science and detail? This isn't a major issue, it just seems surprising. Especially when you point the camera at something that is too dark for the limited exposure capability of the 3.3x tele lens, and it jumps to a zoomed in version of the main camera lens instead. Seriously- see my video for a demonstration of that. You see the color suddenly shift into something that looks very different whenever it changes. The main zoomed in actually looks better, and it has enough native pixels to resolve a decent image... which then begs the question of why even have a dedicated 3.3x tele lens?

4) The notifications in the shade don't let you jump to the application... only individual messages. For example, if I have a bunch of Gmail messages, I can see them in the shade and click them individually to go to them each. But I can't just go to Gmail and see my inbox. Sometimes I want to see my inbox and decide what to respond to first. I have to either go to an individual message, or back out and find the Gmail icon to click it directly.

All in all, the phone is usable but I just can't shake the feeling that the OS is half baked and not ready for release yet. The Android Auto issues and Google Voice ones are so major to the way I use my phone on a daily basis, I might prefer to go back to a device from 3 years ago than continue using this one. It just feels unpredictable and unreliable in its current state. I really do hope Oneplus fixes those bugs soon, because the hardware really is nice. Or better yet, give us the option to run a stock Android without all this OOS nonsense. The customizations aren't a selling point, they are detrimental at best and downright BREAK CERTAIN FUNCTIONALITY at worst. I will gladly change my review and update the rating if an update that addresses these issues comes around. Come on, Oneplus. We know you can do better than this on a phone that costs this much.

Let's get one thing straight right away: THESE ARE NOT SUNGLASSES. They are blue-light blocking at best, or just mildly tinted most likely. I took them out of the box and thought "Oh cool! These are the kinds of glasses that get dark outside and transparent when you are inside!", but nope- I wore them for a full hour outside and they didn't get any darker or exhibit any sun blocking properties AT ALL. So that's false advertising right there. They aren't for use in the sun. They don't darken anything.
As far as audio quality... they are a cool concept, but again, falls short of expectations. The open ear design means the speakers have to work harder to be audible. That means they often make those tin-sounding rattles that tiny speakers make when cranked up too high. This is definitely NOT cool for music as most of the fidelity is lost right off the bat, and adding insult to injury is that they often don't get loud enough to use outside. I'm not saying using it in a crowded subway terminal (that you can just forget about completely), I'm talking about even just going for a stroll around my suburban block with some birds chirping and the wind blowing lightly, maybe a car driving in the distance. I tried listening to a recorded lecture (since music was a lost cause), and they couldn't get loud enough to hear clearly. The microphone for calls was OK in my test, so I guess they are cool as a way to take a phone call without wearing a headset, but that only works if you're wearing these anyway as sunglasses. They aren't sunglasses, so you wouldn't be wearing them anyway, and you wouldn't be wearing them for music, and you wouldn't be wearing them to make a phone call either because they rarely get loud enough unless you are home alone... in which case you can put your phone on speaker and avoid this whole mess.
In conclusion- its a good idea but executed poorly and does NOT live up to expectations. I'm surprised there are so many good reviews on this product. I can't think of a time I would use it.

As someone who works with cameras for a living, I tend to occasionally misplace/lose my lens caps. Having a one-size-fits-all backup like this claims to be, is therefore intriguing to me.
What I found however, is that this fits alright for smaller sized primes (such as those with a front element of 52mm), but a lot of my zooms or larger primes with bigger front elements are difficult or impossible to fit over. Rear cap was also somewhat of a hit-or-miss; I own E-mount, EOS, Nikon F, Minolta A-mount and Micro4/3 lenses, and none of them are too large in their rear element, but some lenses get wide right after the mount and won't allow a cover like this to squeeze over easily. Some of the smaller primes, especially pancake lenses like the Canon 40mm STM, really can't fit both a front and rear "cap" like this since the entire lens would be engulfed in one end or the other.
On top of all that, even if it DOES fit over your lens, I'm cynical as to how how useful it really is. The purpose of a lens cap is to protect the glass from two things: getting dirty and getting damaged. For starters, the material is soft and won't prevent a hard object collision. I'm not exactly willing to test that theory but considering I can press in and feel the glass through the cover, I'm guessing a hard object in your camera bag could still hit it and crack/shatter/damage it. Perhaps the rubber would soften the blow, but a real lens cap would prevent any blow from happening in the first place!
For dust and debris protection, perhaps it is a little useful, however this sort of material tends to attract a lot of static cling. Just leaving it in my gear bag for a bit, I'm finding dust and hair clinging to it like a balloon. Now, it is possible that means the dust/debris will stick to the cap and not your lens, which is useful, however it doesn't give me a lot of confidence to see stuff stuck to the thing I'm about to use to protect my lens from more of that stuff.

I suppose it's good as a backup in my gearbag in case I lose another lens cap and want something to keep dust off it until I get a replacement, but otherwise I'd strongly recommend getting a proper front and end cap for your lenses.

I was trying to setup a studio for a multi-cam live Q&A web-broadcast, and this unit came highly recommended. Turns out this might not be the best choice, and the whole experience sort of leaves a bad taste in my mouth.
First the good:
The functionality of this device really impressed me! All I wanted was a live HDMI switch that would let me keep the audio separate (so it would be live regardless of camera active) and wouldn't blank the display when swapping inputs (which consumer hdmi switches do, as the connection re-negotiates). This unit goes far beyond that, using industry standard production controls for cuts and cross fades, title / graphic overlays, and even some basic Chroma Keying for doing live green screen (that was a surprise!). The little LCD is pretty neat too.
And now, THE BAD:
THERE IS NO HDMI OUTPUT. It only supports SDI, which no one mentioned to me when I said I wanted to toggle between HDMI sources. There is an HDMI preview which shows you multi-view (all the cameras in a grid), but no regular HDMI output. Only SDI, which is ridiculous to me. You have the HDMI port there, at least give us the option to choose whether it is multi-view or program out! Black Magic claims they didn't offer the HDMI out because the connection isn't reliable, so they want to push SDI as the output. But that isn't acceptable, the hardware is there, give us a choice! The result of this stream is going to an internet broadcaster which supports an HDMI input only! Now I'd need to purchase yet another accessory to convert the final product back into an HDMI signal so it can get where it needs to go.
Oh, and speaking of additional accessories that need to be purchased, THE BOX LACKS A POWER CORD. You have to source your own. That seems silly, its such an inexpensive thing that you expect to be there. Thankfully I have a cord from an old lighting accessory that I don't use anymore, but it seemed very odd that it was missing to me. Then, it did not come with a setup guide or instructions, only an SD card. That's fine, going green and all that, but I put it in my laptop and it came up blank. So now I have to find the software and manual myself. And at first, I found what I thought was the correct manual via Google only to realize it was for a different version of their ATEM products.
I know this is an inexpensive product for what it is, but let's be serious for a moment- it still costs nearly $1,000. For that amount of money, how much could it really cost to throw in a power cable and printed manual? $5? 10? Compared to the price of the unit, that's close to nothing. I also know that the buttons on front are because it is designed to be rack-mountable, but when you're setting this up on the fly and try to put on a tabletop, the controls are just awkward. It would have been a lot nicer ergonomically to have some controls on the top instead of the front side. But now that's just nitpicking. At the end of the day, I feel like this device is frustratingly close to what I was looking for, but the experience has been pretty crummy so far.

I've written their technical support for assistance and this is what they told me after a few emails back and forth explaining my issue and running their tests. Here is their final reply, I didn't put in the agents name as to not hold the agent responsible directly for this issue.

(Bragi)
Apr 5, 10:26 CEST
Hello Derek

Thanks for getting back to us with the results of your test.

I understand The Black Dash has some issues when being connected to an external device via Bluetooth, specifically when using it outside. In certain cases we have had a few customers who experienced similar issues like you. As you performed the range test and got a positive result, we can confidently say that your unit's Bluetooth hardware is generally working correctly.

Nonetheless, this is not an excuse for your Bluetooth dropouts. Bluetooth, in general is a technology that offers us the possibility to pair The Black Dash to many different devices, due to the technology's widespread usage. Never the less, it is also a technology that comes with disadvantages. One of those is the actual dependency of the surroundings as you discovered already. That actually means that Bluetooth works very well in closed surroundings where you have surfaces that reflect the Bluetooth signals. However, when being outside with no walls at all, the Bluetooth range very much varies. Having your external device in your right side pockets, your The Black Dash should work independently from the outside surroundings.

Again, this is not an excuse for your Bluetooth dropouts, but rather an explanation for this behavior. Furthermore, we are doing our best to regulate Bluetooth performance with our firmware settings, and every update should actually improve Bluetooth performance.
We hope you can understand that.

All the best,

Pros: Cheap price, handles 4 inputs (would love to see more). One of the [very few inexpensive options] to extract and output a pure digital audio signal (coaxial) rather than the lossier and worse standard- optical. Basically does what it is supposed to do, which is rare these days. Remote control functionality works fine.

Cons: Cheap. Input/output ports are made out of cheap stuff. Need to tweak a little to get the most out of it. Spacing is tight like a manhattan studio. The unit is lightweight and small so it shifts around when you have big cables. Sometimes it gets lost and doesn't do what it is supposed to do- switch. In which case you just have to restart, but it doesn't happen very often. Check video connection if there is an issue as well, which may prevent from switching.

Putting it together: All that being said, its great at this price doing what it is supposed to do, which is hard to say these days with all the ill manufactured things these days. There is nothing out there that will do what it does- 4 x switch PLUS outputting audio via digital coax. At this price point its great for people who dont really care about maximizing the quality of their output. For those who do, like me, not the best but its the only option at this point. Id be more than glad to pay a bit more for a unit with quality input/output ports with a more substantial case. Seems manufacturers these days think all people want are cheap products. There are enough people out there who would pay a bit more for a more quality product. They should consider a two tier product lineup- and not just for the functions. Since there is room for improvement, it gets 4 stars. Make some changes- Ill buy it, and assuming it works, it gets 5 stars.

UPDATE: down to 3 stars. Right at the 30 day mark, the one feature that differentiated this product from others- coax output, stopped working. I did get it replaced and it works. This is somewhat expected, given the quality of material used and the price paid for something like this. Another 30 days and this gets thrown out with the trash for good. At least Amazon has a great policy to protect against something like this. So its worth a shot if you need these features.

UPDATE 2: 2nd time it malfunctioned within a month. Video stopped outputting. When it works, its fine. They really need to use more quality parts in this to make it last. Raise the price a few bucks if necessary. The parts themselves dont cost much. Too much penny pinching. This is getting ridiculous.

UPDATE 3: really save yourself the hassle, frustration and money. Get a pro hdmi switcher. It costs more BUT the output quality and just as important, build quality, is much better. After switching over to a pro, I havent had a hardware issue in 3 months.

What I thought I was getting was a competent mid-level machine that could comfortably replace a four year computer that was barely limping along anymore. Opening files, moving or copying them are all painfully slow. Even deleting files takes a long, dragged out time. Programs freeze even if I'm only running one. Forget running multiple programs at once - the machine just locks up. Videos stutter and freeze. Music stops and starts. The list of slow, clunky issues goes on and on. Even worse is the bugginess. If I switch jacks between speakers and headphones, no sound comes out and the indicators tell me no audio output is plugged in even though one clearly is. It takes 2-3 reboots before the computer figures out that yes, the speakers really are plugged in. Then there's the internet - or the lack thereof. At first I kept getting constant disconnects. That deteriorated to the point where now I can't log in at all. The wifi indicator says I'm connected at full strength. The network troubleshooter says there are no problems. All drivers are up to date. The firewall rules are correctly set. Norton Security, Windows Defender and Malwarebytes all say there is nothing bad lurking in my system. All of that and the machine simply won't connect. The Chrome browser just keeps saying websites can't load, pages can't open, because there is no internet connection. (This review is being written on another computer logged into the same network, one that connects just fine. So the issue is not the router, the isp provider or anything like that.)

As a 69 year old with significant physical issues, the thought of reboxing this piece of junk up and hauling it to a shipper to return it feels overwhelming. EDIT: And the return process through UPS was a horrific mess. I stopped at the UPS store a couple of days ahead of time to ask them if they could box the computer and monitor up for me if I brought in all the original boxes and packing material. The nice young man working that afternoon said of course though he would have to charge me a dollar for tape. Two days later when I brought everything to the store, a different staff member said they had to charge me $30 for boxes even though I had brought the boxes in. Not only that, but I had forwarded the shipping label to that UPS store via email. They couldn't open the label so I had to go home, print out a screenshot of the label and send them that. The kicker though was that I couldn't leave the computer and monitor at the store while I ran home, ten minutes away. The clerk insisted that I carry it all out to the car again and then carry it back into the store when I returned. For somebody of my age with my health issues, that is not a trivial thing. The last time I tried to return something through UPS they gave me such a run around that I ended up throwing the item away rather than return it to Amazon. The hassle was more than the product was worth. If I ever have to return anything again, I'll ask Amazon if I can do it through Fed Ex or the Post Office. UPS is too much hassle.

*UPDATE ON REVIEW AFTER A FEW DAYS OF USE.
After installing the unit and using it for a few days it now has pop up ads on screen and wants you to purchase subscription services for extra features that were not mentioned in the description of the item. The ads make the unit difficult and unsafe to use while driving. We would not recommend this product.

ORGINAL INSTALL REVIEW BEFORE THE POP-UP ADS.
Pros: As the headline says, everything you need to install is included in the box including a backup camera and GPS antenna. The wire harness adapter is pre-wired to plug the unit directly into your factory harness/plugs without splicing any wires. It mounts directly up to the stock radio location without the use of any installation adapters or cutting plastics. The stock plastic trim plate aligns perfectly over the unit once installed and keeps a clean factory look. Optional RCA plug wire harnesses and USB tether plugs are also included for compatibility with your own custom aftermarket external sound equipment if needed. It works with both Apple CarPlay and Android Auto enabled cell phones. It can be used as a mobile Wi-Fi internet hotspot for passengers when paired with your cellphone. System updates can be downloaded directly to the unit through home or cell Wi-Fi once installed. If you have steering wheel controls, they can be manually programed from a menu on the unit to do the functions intended.

Cons: Menus are a little confusing and hard to find "while doing the initial radio setup". The EQ setting screen is hard to find and the HiFi setting (which acts a volume/bass boost) should be turned off if are using stock factory Jeep speakers. HiFi is turned on by default and it makes the volume level far too loud on the stock speakers at its lowest possible volume knob setting. Once the EQ and HiFi 0n/0ff settings are set to your ideal preferences you won’t need to navigate to the EQ screen again. Last minor con is when/how you exit your installed Aps. You’ll need to swipe them completely off the screen to stop them from running in the background and slowing the unit down similar to a cellphone.

Overall: Lots of features. Easy downloadable state maps for NAVI. Easy to download updates. Sounds better than the stock Jeep CD player once the EQ setting have been adjusted. Has a microphone intergraded into the faceplate. Easy to customize the display brightness, colors, wallpaper, and sounds. All the buttons/knobs are backlit with your headlight activation. It will play movies and MP3s.

I found Bose's latest wireless headphones to be a fairly serious disappointment, which was surprising and frustrating after having bought 5 or 6 pairs of headphones over the years, along with speakers and a Wave Radio. I *like* Bose products.

Let me start with the positive, to be fair.

1. They sound great.
2. They stay in my ears. (A feature Apple did not think to include with their glorious AirPods.)
3. The Bose connect app on the iPhone is slick and useful.

The negatives.

1. They are very big and jut from my ears in a way that looks comical. I've seen other people compare them to the bolts on Frankenstein's neck, but for the ears. Actually, though, it's worse than that, because their weight makes them droop. So I'd describe the look as more Frankenstein Eeyore. If you have hair that covers your ears, you will probably be ok. But I am close to bald, so I can't really wear them in public. Since I bought them to wear during my workouts at LA Fitness and while coding at work, the fact that they make me look silly is a show stopper.

2. Given the look issues, I'd love to wear them when I listen to music on my computer at home, but they don't pair properly with Windows 10. They have a voice profile and a music profile. No matter how I fiddle with my PC, based on advice from the various threads on Bose's support forums, I cannot get the music profile to activate. The reason this is a problem is that the voice profile only plays music in one ear, and at far reduced quality. Like it's-being-piped-to-your-ear-through-Satan's-toilet quality. Bose's suppport forums have various threads about this, and it's clear that some part of Bose's software group either doesn't get it or is trying to avoid publicly stating that they can't fix the problem. They claim it is Windows or software differences on various PCs, but my Apple AirPods work fine as do Bose's SoundSport Wireless headphones (though they lack a mic, so the scenario is somewhat different).

3. I wish there was a way to hear audio in both ears while making calls. You can do this with the AirPods.

I waited some time to review these because I tried on various occasions to install them. It was a total bust.

WHAT ARE THESE LIKE?
These covers come in a plastic bag with a little clear plastic box attached to a card. Inside there are three covers. Each is covered with a clear blue plastic sheet.

HOW ARE THEY SUPPOSED TO WORK?
You clean off the spot you are supposed to put it on.
You remove the plastic back
Press into place
Wait 24 hours
Slide door back and forth when you want to use the camera.

HOW DOES THIS PERFORM
OMG what a frustration! First of all, these do not stay together long enough to press them to the laptop! Before I can even press them into place, the "slide" cover pops out. If I stick the back to the laptop, the door won't go in. If I have the door in place, when I stick the back to the laptop, the door won't slide AT ALL and ends up popping out.

If I get frustrated and try to take it off, it pops off the laptop.

We are very satisfied with the two DIR-655s that we have (at two sites). They hold up well and cause no problems. They're fast and stable; they run cool and basically require little or no attention.

Two router features that deserve much more discussion than they usually get are the unit's firewall (if any) and its Quality-of-Service (QoS) engine (if any).

o The firewall keeps external probes and hack-attempts out of your network. You'd be amazed how many probes a home or business broadband connection gets every hour from places like China, Eastern Europe and the Middle East. They're looking for ways in so they can infect your machines and steal your information. A router with a good firewall implemented in its firmware is increasingly essential. Firewalls let internal users establish connections with remote machines, not the other way around. And the DIR-655's firewall is excellent, a stateful-packet-inspection implementation that is truly industrial-class. Frankly, I didn't know this when I bought my first unit but was delighted to discover it once I brought it home. Good stuff. And, it's compatible with my company's virtual-private-network (VPN) approaches, which can be a real problem for firewalls to accommodate. My company has used two VPN approaches in the time I've had our DIR-655s, and there have been no issues.

o A good QoS engine prioritizes time-critical Internet traffic such as voice-over-Internet (VoIP). I did not fully appreciate this until we pulled the plug on our landline and implemented "roll-your-own VoIP", saving 90% off our monthly phone costs (see [...] for details). Only a router with good QoS capabilities will allow phone calls to be clear, crisp and smooth in the face of other Internet traffic. And the DIR-655 turns out to have a very good QoS engine. It automatically prioritizes the standard VoIP ports so our phone calls sound as good as a landline even with two teenagers streaming video, cruising Facebook, listening to Pandora, Skyping and FaceTime-ing, etc. Unfortunately, the marketplace is not yet fully aware of the benefits of a good QoS engine in routers, so it's not a given. Even Apple's well-regarded and excellent Time Capsule and Airport/Airport Extreme routers don't have it, for example. But DIR-655 does.

The only issue we've ever experienced with the DIR-655s in our years of usage was once when a cell phone got into a conniption loop that had it disassociate and reassociate with the router over and over and over again, many times per minute. This caused the router to bog down and reboot itself (and who could blame it). The DIR-655's informative logs helped me diagnose what was going on. Eventually the phone got straightened out, and the problem went away.

UPDATE: I can no longer recommend this router. The latest firmware is abysmal and ruins what was formerly a good product.

Having had no problems with the first one (other than the occasional background static or need to switch frequencies, as mentioned by other reviewers), I immediately went out and bought another one to replace it. The only difference I could see between them was that the first one was black and the new one was silver and black. At any rate, it worked great for a while. They had superior bass, great music sound, and I didn't have to open the box to see the charge status. Phone calls worked fine. Fit all good like my former K23's from a different brand. Case is larger and heavier than with those.

I got a low power message. Okay I left them to charge. There were no indicator lights. Oh well. The next morning they were not charged! I got a low power message again but checked and the case was to 98% full! Well I don't need technical difficulty, there was no wiggle room in the holder, I'm not putting up with this! and I ordered my old brand.

When I opened the new (old) pair the sticker instructed me to remove the little strips of plastic that were across the metal charging points on the earbuds that make contact with the case points. Ohhhhh... Do you suppose? Could be?...

When I got home, just in case, I got out these new pair from the box again and opened the case and took out the bud and... I see. I hate to write this review, since these have the best sound I've heard comparing to Sony (wired) 7506s. The sound on these is excellent. It's everything else that fails, eventually causing me to return them after a couple days. I'm currently trying Cowin E7s.

The humorously deep ear pads aren't bad and that's where I think they get most if their bass response from, as the "extra" deep bass is non-existent as far as the electronics are concerned. To repeat, these are absolutely not for bassheads. Nothing like Anker. I'm not a basshead so this worked out for me. Panasonic repeatedly gets an almost Sony sound; bright highs and balanced mids.

However they did press against my temples a little too much and I can see them causing someone a headache after awhile. Again I'm not susceptible so it wasn't a problem for me. The bluetooth, unfortunately, has interrupts about every 20 minutes. Unlike others, I have never experienced this phenomena with any other bluetooth device or phone. My inexpensive Mpows don't do this. And, sigh, the stupid bass switch RATTLES. With loud volume and pop/rock bass you won't hear it. Listening to classical or jazz with these would be impossible. They creak. The plastic is super lightweight, cheaply built, and poorly designed. Trying to enjoy music in a rocking chair after awhile will get to you. Again none of my other headphones do this.

Bottom line, super balanced sound (NOT bassy despite their advertising) but poorly designed with cheap materials and subpar bluetooth which defeats enjoying the great sound. Really too bad.

This is the first and probably only time I could afford a Grundig related radio. I'm sorry to report all the other comments are true, especially the negative ones. My main problem is it's basically unusable because of the controls on every edge and side of the radio. It has two wheel knobs on one side for volume and manual tuning which is good because without autoprogramming or presets the button tuning process is hair-pulling frustration. You have to go to each station, one at a time, to get anywhere on the dial. And there's no direct entry. That leaves the side-wheel which of course changes the frequency every time you pick it up or put it in a pocket. Volume likewise. The band selector opposite edge is very stiff and you cannot switch to a specific shortwave or AM band with any accuracy. It also mutes sound while tuning so you won't know if there's a faint signal to be heard unless you wait a second on every frequency. The autoscan bypasses most AM stations including local moderately strong ones. If you do take the time the actual AM reception isn't bad, just tuning is tiring. Reception on shortwave is far better with my cheap handhelds. The stereo signal on FM has a problem and even strong local stations are usually monaural. Even when it's on the stereo field is almost absent.

It sounds very good (don't expect bass), clear, loud bluetooth sound,  not softer than the radio sound and that's the last good thing I have to say about it. [Great Sound]

As noted in some of the other reviews this pair of headphones has great sound for its price range. Sound is quite neutral, without the bass emphasis of a lot of headphones at this range. Highs are also good and not muted. The cable is also very generous in length, which is great as my computer is far away from my chair. Finally, the headband adjustment is exceptional. I have a fairly large skull and most headphones I've purchased have not fit well. However, this one fits perfectly and even has more room to expand. The only comfort downside is that the pads have quite a stiff covering material. This is not so great for comfort for long use sessions, but not too big of an issue as you can replace them eventually if needed. The thicker pad material would make the headphones last longer...if it were not for the major issue I describe below with build quality.

[Disappointing Build Quality]

I've had my pair for about 1.5 years now, and today the headphone snapped at the joint between the top band and where the extension band slides out. See attached photo. You can see that there is a metal band in the headband to provide elasticity and resistance. But the extension band (the part that slides in and out) doesn't have a metal band inside of it. This concentrates stress at this transition point, causing the plastic to snap here eventually. I noticed that the plastic on the other cup has also started cracking. The plastic itself feels quite brittle and is about as thick as the metal strip in the headband. I think the fact that I have a large head and had to extend the headphones out only hastened their demise as this put more stress on the plastic-only part of the headbands.

[Conclusion]

This is a great sounding pair of headphones for their price, but alas I cannot recommend them anymore due to the snapping of the headband. To fail after about a year of use is a bit on the low end. My previous pair of similarly priced headphones lasted over 10 years without the headband failing (only cable had become worn). I think you *might* be OK if you have a smaller head and don't have to extend the headphone band too much, but if you have to expand it to near its maximum, it will probably snap off like mine did.

Both the image and audio quality from this camera have always been disappointing. I didn't really know just how poor it was until I owned an iPhone 4S, which captures vastly superior video, and mono audio that sounds much better than the tinny stereo captured by the Picsio.

And then there's the problem with mysteriously aborted video recordings, which has happened twice to me. The first time I missed part of a dance performance, but that was mostly an annoyance at the time, since it was an ad-hoc recording and I simply switched to my phone. The second time, I missed a good chunk of a recital I'd been asked to video for a friend. The recording stopped unexpectedly and retained only 1 second of the segment. I had started the recording, watched a few seconds to confirm that it going, and sat down. 9 minutes later someone notified me that the display had gone black and it hadn't been blinking for the previous two songs. When I hit the power button and it woke up (!?!?), the display said something about "file" and "management" and "update", and after trying to get it to come on and start recording, it said "update complete" or "finished" and then it recorded the remainder of the performance. (Pardon me if I don't remember the exact on-screen messages.) I had an hour of capacity (in iFrame mode) left on the card, which was freshly formatted, and the camera was on DC power so that batteries wouldn't be an issue. There was no discernible reason for this to have happened.

Bottom line: I can't trust this camera, and I won't even try to resell it or give it to someone; I wouldn't want to do that to someone else. For more serious video, I dropped the coin on a Canon VIXIA (which is fantastic), and for casual video, I'll use my iPhone. Either way, I will never rely on this camera again.

I have heard about complaints regarding Asus poor customer support (which I had experienced myself with a mobo I bought recently and could not get in months any response about a question I posted). It all boiled down to an exercise on probabilities: chances were the laptop would work fine, if not I would have to return it, not counting on Asus for anything.

After that I have another big surprise: the hinge that keeps together keyboard and screen does not have a connector (they are connected wiressly) which leaves the problem of charging the smaller battery on the keyboard part. A third, odd thing was that the speakers (which sounded awful, BTW) are located on one side of the screen.
I ended up returning it and buying instead a Lenovo Yoga 2 Pro for $1,200. Cheaper, with the same CPU, memory and HDD, and with a better-that-Retina 3200x1800 screen (instead of the FullHD 1080). Plus, it is designed properly.

In full disclosure, I must admit that I miss my Bose Bluetooth speaker. Their acoustics are impeccable. The "Tribit XSound Go Bluetooth Speakers" only cost a fraction of my Bose speaker. I first purchased the "DOSS Touch Wireless Bluetooth" which is in the same price range; I returned that product because it lacked bass and was unimpressive overall. The Tribit, however, has plenty of bass for such a small speaker. Ironically, the problem that I have is the treble! I think it is an inherent problem with smaller speakers and not this particular device. I have installed an equalizer on my computer which mitigates some of the problems and makes the speaker sound very acceptable.

The pros:
• The speaker is loud! It is perfect for a jam session in your bedroom. I'm not sure it is suitable for large or multi rooms.
• The quality is good, and the speaker looks like a million bucks.
• It has an excellent microphone that works well with phone calls and even to interact with Siri or Cortana.
• The Play button allows one to answer, reject or end a call. It also can play or pause a song. Finally, it allows you to skip a music track forward or backward.

The cons:
• While the bass is fairly impressive, the treble is slightly overriding.
• The battery does not nearly last for 24 hours if you like to blast music as I do
• The speaker can only be paired to one device at a time. If you are listening to music on the computer and the phone tries to connect, the speaker will sometimes disconnect from all devices. The speaker does have an av input one could connect to the computer but obviously, the speaker would no longer be completely portable. This could be a deal breaker for many.

After comparing this speaker with others in its price range, I realize that this speaker has such poor sound quality that I could never recommend it to anyone.

Update: After less than 60 days of owning the TV, the ENTIRE audio panel died. None of the external audio ports work anymore for no reason whatsoever. Worked fine, then boom just stopped working. Thought it was my soundbar, so I bought a new soundbar, but nope, soundbar works just fine when connected to the cable box. Amazon Prime was awesome in helping me return it, and I'll be picking up a more reliable brand. When it came time to purchase a new TV we approached it the same way we approached buying a house. We made a list of the features we wanted (a SmartTV with Wifi, streaming channels, Amazon Prime, 40” and affordable at around the $250 mark). After looking at our options in terms of price and convenience, we decided that it made the most sense to purchase it through Amazon Prime.

After much research, we decided that the TCL TV’s offered the best value, met our budget requirements, and our decision to purchase the TV through Amazon enabled us to purchase the TV with interest free financing over 6 months.
Appearance.
The TV came in a large box with the stand hardware: remote, power cable and batteries plus simple instructions that were in separate bags. You do not get a HDMI or any other cables. The TV has a simple non-fussy design with approximately half inch bezel all around. The stand that comes with it is simple and screws on with two screws at each side. The stand footprint requires about 8.5 inches of depth to stand on. I like that the stand is low profile raising the screen about 2” above the surface it is standing on.

Setup

The old analog phono inputs are on the back and quite hard to reach once the TV is up on the mantle and they protrude straight out the back which would require more space between the wall and the TV if you use them. The power cable plugs into a recessed area low down on the left side and doesn’t interfere with the location of the tv. All the modern input and output sockets are behind the screen on the right side about 8 inches back. We don’t use any subscription TV service; just a double bowtie antenna mounted on one of the gutter pipes at the back of the house. The coaxial input for the antenna along with three HDMI ports, an optical input, 3.5mm jack and USB socket are all here. We use two of the HDMI sockets one for the 1TB Media hub and the other for our notebook.

Once everything is plugged in and turned on. The TV introduces you to the basic setup process. It takes less than five minutes to find your way around. The remote is minimalist with the most basic controls on the front (Volume Up/Down toggle and mute buttons on the side). It’s small, unfussy and easy to use. The UI for the TV is not flashy but functional and easy to navigate. Setting up WIFI, registering your TV and introducing you to streaming channels and how to add them to your desktop are covered quickly and then you are left to your own devices.

Since we are just using an antenna we were initially a little apprehensive. Wondering how well that would work, or even if the TV had a tuner since everyone seems to use dish or cable these days. It has a tuner that works flawlessly. We managed to pick up almost 3 dozen channels many of them HD. A quick look online showed us a map of where the broadcast towers are and helped us aim our antenna for best reception.

In use.

The TV has a really nice clean picture and since it is an LED TV where a grid array of LED's light the screen uniformly rather than a couple of fluorescent lamps there is practically no limit to the viewing angle. The screen is not high gloss and prevents reflection and most glare from bright light sources. When turned on a non invasive 3” horizontal strip of illuminated plastic at the bottom shows you the TV is powered on. It flashes during startup and goes out when the screen is illuminated.

Image

Image quality is excellent BUT on initial setup it is on a bright echo setting. Which is very high contrast and overly saturated. I guess it is a power saving mode (claimed 16 watts) but it is a bit stark and overwhelming and shows some dithering on smooth color transitions as though it is running at a lower bitrate with fewer colors. When turned to theater mode the quality of the picture is MUCH better with very smooth transitions on subtle colour gradients.

Sound

Sound is similar. Like most LCD style TV’s this one comes with tiny speakers. Again the default sound setting seems to be very flat. Probably to conserve energy. There are about four presets and again we went with theater which gives the broadest range and warm midtones without overdoing the bass. It doesn’t sound too bad and is not thin and reedy like the default setting.

Smart TV functionality.

We originally wanted WIFI because as Amazon Prime members we get a lot of free on demand media. This is similar to Netflix where you can watch a huge catalog of TV and movies for free, buy or rent them for a small fee. The same goes with music. This worked perfectly.

What we weren’t expecting was the sheer volume of streaming media available for free via WIFI. There are hundreds of channels, many of them free to choose from, many mainstream ones that let you view their current episodes of popular shows on demand when you want to watch them. You can also sign up for pay for view services like HBO and showtime individually.

One nice thing is that the TV has a global search option. You can search for anything by title, director, actors name, character, keywords and the TV will find everything relating to your search and list what is available by channel. So you can easily pick out what you want to see.

Mobile devices and streaming from those devices

There are apps for Android and iOS as well as Windows. I was able to control the TV from all our devices. In many ways it is more responsive, especially if you need to type in text. If you have media on your PC there are Apps for the TV that will let you stream from your phone, notebook, desktop computer etc.

Streaming from those devices tends to work ok. I did find that the TV’s built-in media player was a little limited in supported data formats. Setting up our digital media hub with its own channel was very easy and luckily our Western Digital media hub has far more extensive support for many of the more exotic file formats like FLAC lossless digital audio. And other formats are more often limited to computers. The TV does support the more mainstream formats like mp3, mpg, jpg etc.

Conclusion

For us, this TV proved to be a very good and affordable purchase. Especially when you factor in the 6 months interest fee financing Amazon offers prime members. We did sign up for a free month of Netflix too. The remote has a dedicated Netflix and Amazon streaming button. But we were not that impressed with Netflix when our Amazon Prime membership offered all the same features and more thanks to the addition of Amazon Prime music.

When you combine all this TV’s features with our media hub and Amazon Prime we are a bit overwhelmed with the sheer amount of stuff out there to watch. Even if we had no antenna and just a WIFI internet connection. The vast number of free streaming HD channels is extensive making the need for TV subscription plans pretty much obsolete unless you have a very specific need.

We really like this TV and highly recommend it.

They however do look oem quality.

Either I got a different product or the people reviewing here are fake on not very skillfully discriminating.

While these may actually be OEM(??), they are hard and uncomfortable, not super-duper plush/soft/comfortable like the original ones I have. And, they sound wrong.

I also own the closed back, HD598CE. They have hard pads, as they are designed for monitoring, to not let sound leak by the pads into your ears so you can discern the music in your headphones from ambient sound and to keep feedback from blowing your ears out. And, like when you record singing or playing guitar while monitoring a track, and you don't want the stuff playing in your headphones to leak out and get picked up on the mic. You need harder, denser pads for this. But, they are way less comfortable with less sound-stage and more bass. ...Just like the pads sold here.

tldr: these are much harder (less comfortable) than original HD598SE/SR pads and feel more like pads on the closed back HD598CE. And, sounds more bassy, less sound-stage, lower mids/highs.

Bought two Play 5's directly from Sonos and have been testing them out for over a week now.

First the good —to my knowledge —there isn't better multi-room home audio setup out there, not at this price point. But if you're reading this you probably already knew that. Setup is fast and easy, you can join / separate "rooms" on the fly and guests can add songs seamlessly (once they know how to use the controller app).

But here's what you need to know about the revamped Play 5 — the audio quality just isn't that great, not for $500 / speaker. The new Play 5 sounds airy, flat and lacks definition throughout. I'm disappointed because it's been 6 years since the Play 5 (named the ZonePlayer S5 in 2009) first launched and while the 2015 update improves audio quality it doesn't compare to wireless offerings from B&W. Are my standards high? Absolutely. But so are Sonos's.

I really wanted to like the Play 5’s, for most listeners it will be a great addition to a Sonos household (most people who buy Sonos already own at least 1 speaker). Today many people are perfectly happy with compressed audio and disposable ear buds – the Play 5 reinforces this trend. It comes down to a tradeoff do you need multi-room home audio? If so, you’ll probably be better off with Sonos if you don’t mind sacrificing audio quality. If audio quality is higher up on your list look elsewhere – B&W is a great place to start, or ditch wireless all together.

If all you watch is driven by an external device like a cable box or Roku or something, then this is probably an acceptable TV for you. However, you're paying a good chunk of money to have a "smart" TV that can connect to services like Netflix, Amazon Prime Video, and Hulu, and that "smart" technology is terrible.

- The video streaming apps crash regularly, or go unresponsive, or will have significant delays, or even lock up so badly that you have to reboot the TV. And since there's no volume-equalizing feature, sometimes a quiet TV show will crash and abruptly you'll be sent back to the default "TV Plus" music channels, blaring a country song at ear-splitting volumes.

- Those same apps sometimes receive forced updates without any notice. One day you'll turn on the TV and discover that the controls are different or even missing. For example, my son loves the "Classical Baby" series via Amazon, and would frequently used the "restart season from the beginning" button to watch it again. Then one day, poof, no more button. To watch it again, we have to navigate back to the first episode, resume it (which picks up about 4 seconds from the end), and quickly start rewinding all the way back to the beginning of the episode. This itself is not a huge deal but the same type of unexpected, forced-on-you changes have happened many times in the last 2 years of owning the TV.

- The "dynamic" picture mode looks good on a few shows but on others will seriously distort colors. Skin will be bluish, or someone's red coat will be super-saturated into a weird blob of red on the screen. It also increases the refresh rate so things suddenly lose the normal movie feel and instead get that soap opera feel to them.

- It doesn't support the normal phone "cast" features that pretty much every other TV and phone supports. It supposedly supports a screen mirroring feature via their own SmartThings mobile app but the configuration is so awful and inconsistent that I have yet to get any casting to work (I'm a techie so these things are not often difficult). Why wouldn't they just go with the normal way that everyone else does it, which works flawlessly? Who knows.

Maybe in the future, Samsung will get their act together but right now it's a very bad buy for most people.

MY HISTORY WITH THIS PRODUCT:
I've owned this headset for almost a full year. Technically, I've had two of them, since the boom mic snapped off the first one and had it replaced. I use these every day, for multiple hours and a variety of uses (VoIP calls, gaming, music, and movies).

PROS:
The audio quality, when it is working, is good. The bass in 7.1 mode is great, and the overall surround sound is pretty convincing. They are comfortable and rechargeable via USB.

CONS:
The biggest problem here is the wireless connection. Both headsets I owned suffered from this same problem - they would frequently just restart or lose the signal and reconnect. The process takes about 3-5 seconds each time, and sometimes you get multiple restarts in a row. It doesn't sound too bad until it happens when you're watching a movie and you have to quickly pause or rewind a bit because you suddenly couldn't hear anything they were saying (which also completely pulls you out of the movie), or when it drops out in the middle of a phone conversation, or drops out at the worst possible moment in a game... It happens probably two dozen times a day, if not more. At first, I didn't care too much about it, but the first time you have it drop out 3 times in a matter of a single minute, it's simply maddening. Imagine going randomly deaf for several seconds throughout every day of your life, and you'll get a sense of what it's like.

If I could simply plug the cable in and it would use the USB cable to transmit the audio instead of wireless, that would be perfect, but when it's plugged in, it simply charges the internal battery - you still get audio interruptions all the time. The interruptions will also reset the "mute" status on the mic, which can be troublesome if you're intentionally muted on a conference call and suddenly your mic is on and people hear you eating lunch.

Second problem is that the power button is a bit flaky. If the headset is plugged in via USB and powered off, sometimes it will not power on unless you unplug the headset and THEN power it on (and then you can plug it back in to continue charging). I thought it was a defect in my first headset until the same thing happened with the second one.

A minor third problem is that the boom mic is a little flimsy on the construction. I am careful with my toys, but it still cracked and finally snapped off one day when I was lowering the mic to use it, and that was only a few months into owning it.

OVERALL:
If they would fix the wireless, I would rate this 4 stars in a heartbeat. If they fixed the power button, it would go up to 5. That said, the G35 seems to be the G930 but wired, and cheaper. The number of times that I've wanted to really make good use of the wireless (go to another room and keep the audio going) is far less frequent than the dozens upon dozens of times that the audio cuts out, so it's just an unacceptable point for me, since that is what this headset is about.

When I received this DAC adaptor I was really ready to love it. Like many other late-model iPhone owners I was disappointed in the signal reproduction of Apple's stock Lightening-to-Headphone-Plug adaptor with its cheap DAC and was trying to find a replacement that had a better frequency response and sampling rate. This device, while oddly bulky, seemed to fit the bill. The device has controls for volume and track selection like pretty much all headphones that are designed to be used with smartphones so unless you are using old-school or audiophile headphones all these controls manage to do is render the controls on your headphones inoperable. Considering this means you a reaching for controls that are going to be right next to your phone anyway, it definitely reduces the convenience factor in your controls are located up the wire near so you don't have to fishing for it in your pocket. The devices is well built out of machines aluminum, it's unnecessarily bulky and the short lightening cord makes it awkward and likely to put torsional strain on the lightening port of your iPhone- something you really don't want to do.

But how does it sound?

Initially, I was really impressed with the sound reproduction playing an album that was mixed at a lower gain amplitude, like what you'd find from a streaming service or Apple Music. In combination with my Ultimate Ears TripleFi 10s I was pleased to finally hear the full sound reproduction so that trouble of encoding my music at a 320k bitrate finally wasn't a complete waste of storage space as it was before since the stock adaptor steps bitrate down to something like 192k. (Don't quote me on that.) Anyway, all seemed well, even if the device was kind of bulky and the black finish on the aluminum started to rub off after the first day, until I played some music that was encoded with an unusually high gain. The sounds was UNLISTENABLE. It was so distorted that I was worried I was damaging my headphones. I checked the SoundWise App that you can download to update firmware and boost the signal if need be, but none of that was in use. The DAC simply couldn't handle the signal! Even the cheap Apple adaptor could play that signal without butchering the sound, albeit it in its flat, lossy way that it usually does.

Therefore, I do not recommend this product. I was really hoping to love it and that it would solve the crappy DAC problem Apple created, but it simply was not designed well. Keep looking...

We just went through the worst winter storm in recorded history, down here in Austin Texas. In fact, it's still not over. Power is still out in a lot of areas. And, they're still doing 'rolling blackouts', even in our neighborhood. One of the things that we really depended on, with no power, no cell service, no internet, no NOTHING, was having this NOAA-AM-FM radio that was rechargeable by either cranking it yourself or solar panel. To be honest, I have THREE of these things. One in my truck, her car, and here at home. Some may say that I'm a worry wart. But, I say, better to have it and not need it....

This one, from the YEZRO Store took me a minute to figure out. It's a little different from the others. But, once I finally got it, it's really easy to operate. The flashlight is just bright enough to light your way in a dark house. (Don't expect it to light your path down a long dark road in the country.) The 'alarm' is more amusing than anything. (Really, I laughed.) The tuning knob is DIRECT on a very small tuner. So, you have to go SLOW when scrolling through the band for the best signal. The speaker is kind of small and tinny sounding. It has a battery level indicator LED that does a decent job of letting you know when it's time to recharge. The band selector switch works very well, as does the volume knob. You should know that the telescoping antenna is another way of getting the strongest signal from your chosen station. Radio signals travel up and down the antenna in a 'sign wave', not just to the tip. So, after you do your best with the tuning knob, you can increase or decrease the length of the radial (as well as change the angle) to fine tune it even more. This radio is NOT water proof. So, protect it from rain. The ability to play music from an SD card or a flash drive is a nice feature. But, I consider that kind of pointless in an 'emergency' radio.

I know that I've picked it apart quite a bit. But, looking at the primary function of this radio, and how well it served me in this winter storm, I can really only give it accolades. It did an admirable job. Especially considering the small investment I made in it. I'm glad I have it. And, now, it's going back in it's box and in my closet until the next storm. it gives me a sense of security, just knowing it's there.

What occurred to me after wasting half an hour with this thing is that what is needed is an iPhone app to control your television and stereo, not a single freaking light bulb and a long, long list of codes printed in mouse type.

See photo. The remote looks good, shiny Darth Vader black. There are three manuals, one of which is about an ounce and a half. One is a long list of codes and the third unfolds to about 10x17 so that between the three differently-sized printed manuals you have a lap full of clutter which is difficult to manage while you're trying to press buttons in some order.

I couldn't get it to do much of anything, and by the time I realized that half an hour had gone by and I was getting hot under the collar, I thought: FAIL. Why waste any more of my time? Ah, but by THAT time I was and am good and frustrated at this RCA product. RCA. Who knew they were still in business? Who the heck would buy an RCA product? I'm sure they made great gramophones back in the day, but Sony came by and ate their lunch and even that was forty years ago.

If you were an RCA exec, wouldn't you want to make certain that anything your company made was functional? I've got a couple college degrees. I can tie my own shoes. I can do all kinds of things, but I couldn't figure out how to program this little (EXPLETIVE DELETED) thing. Which frustrates me.

The first thing I noticed (after I cut the I-dare-you-to-open-me hard plastic packaging) was that it hurt to open the battery compartment. There's some idiotic L-shaped trigger you have to depress, meaning that you're digging it under your fingernails, which I think most people would find painful. Just a dumb design move. No other word for it. Dumb.

The remote looks good and has some interesting ribs underneath it. The buttons are not what you might expect, the volume and channel buttons are flabby feeling and weak, not definite-feeling. The center "OK" button is kind of clicky, like cellophane. There's a whole array of buttons, but it's not worth my time to try and program each one. And I grew to dislike the hard plastic feeling of the remote. There are other plastic materials that feel better to the hand. LOOK AT SONY PRODUCTS, RCA, LOOK AT SONY PRODUCTS FOR A FREE CLUE.

I'm annoyed and frustrated. This seemed like such a neat idea. But sitting on my couch juggling three differently-sized manuals AND this remote and wondering why none of these instructions were doing anything was really frustrating, just not how I want to spend my free time. I'll happily continue to exist with my TV remote, my surround-sound remote, my AppleTV remote and the AT&T cable box remote, you know? BECAUSE THEY WORK and they work without frustrating me.

Here's my idea: RCA hires an app developer and somehow figures out how to have your devices tell the app what their codes area. Something like that. Because the notion of combing through a manual full of codes in tiny type is worse than doing your income taxes.

THE WORLD HAS MOVED ON, RCA and you are apparently living in the 1970s with burgundy leisure suits and avocado-colored kitchen appliances.

STAY AWAY FROM THIS REMOTE, IT WILL ONLY FRUSTRATE YOU and dig in the skin under your nails. Ouch. Did this thing really have to be so frustrating? Do you imagine this is the kind of experience consumers are after? Not just one more freaking remote control, but one that promises convenience and delivers frustration? Not a good product. Stay away from it.

I followed the instructions (which were not easy to understand, since they were largely picture based), and plugged it in to my flat iron. Immediately, I heard a buzzing sound and my flat iron melted all the way through in the middle.

Upon returning from my trip (during which I could not plug in any electrical items since my converter was not trustworthy), I notified Amazon and was told that the 30-day return window had closed but they would make a "special exception" and allow me to return it for a refund. They gave me a $20 credit for the "inconvenience", which might have satisfied me for the true inconvenience of not being able to use my phone charger, hair dryer, or now-dead flat iron during the trip. However, they were not willing to compensate me for even part of the $100 to replace my flat iron. I am shocked to see that Amazon does not replace items damaged by their faulty products. I'll think twice about ever buying electronic items from them again!

Even though it looks like a solid turntable built on a wooden slab, all the moving parts and the tone arm are actually mounted on a thin plastic plate that sits in a cavity in the wooden piece. This plastic plate started warping up on the right side after a few months of use and now the turntable is rotating at an uneven rate. If you have any respect for your music and your LPs, spend a bit more and buy one of the Audio Technica turntables.
The audio quality on this webcam is horrible. Audio is very distorted and is full of noise and intermittent breaks. Video quality is worse than the built in (720p) webcam on my laptop.

These are very poorly designed speakers. The specifications which claim a frequency response of 45-20,000Hz +/- 3dB is completely bogus, even at 100Hz, the response is down more than -6dB. I doubt if they can generate any audible audio at 45Hz. And 90dB sensitivity number is pure fiction. They do have relatively crisp highs and they may actually work ok if you are only going to listen to talk radio, but for music, they are hopeless.

Canon AE version does not work with EOS 7D Mark ii or EOS 80D. Cannot control (or see) the aperture even in M mode. Camera gives an error every time I try to take a picture. The AE version does not have a manual aperture ring, so if the AE chip cannot talk to the camera, it is impossible to use it.

P.S. I used the fully manual version of this lens in the past and the optics were quite good (with the exception of distortion), but I was not able to take any shots with the new AE version, so I cannot comment on the optical quality.

Yes, it is noise cancelling, offers excellent sound and pairing - HOWEVER the mechanical design leaves a lot to be desired. The earpiece does not hug your face and with rotate out of your ear canal regardless the ear tip used or how you set it in your ear. The over the ear battery design causes the boom portion to rotate and ultimately making your ear stick out like dumbo as well as the boom wandering out from your face.  It's not comfortable to wear because you're constantly fiddling with it to keep it in place. FAIL

Cheap, unshielded cable. There was so much static that you couldn't hear the music.

It takes a few minutes to boot, and works poorly with the FireStick iPhone app.  When you use an arrow key, there is a noticeable delay from when you press the button to when the screen updates and plays a clicking sound.  The Fire Stick struggles to connect with the app and sometimes won’t connect at all.  The delay is even worse when using Alexa through the remote. I have a Google Pixel 6 smartphone. The title of this product says it works with Google Pixel phones. That is a lie. As soon as I plug this adapter into my phone, I get an error that says the cable only supports analog audio and the phone requires a digital cable with a digital-to-analog (DAC) converter. If you have a modern higher-end Google or Apple or Samsung smartphone, this adapter will not work for you. They are relatively cheap, but they do not work.

I have other adapters with DACs that work fine. Don't buy this one.

With just 3GB of RAM and a low-end CPU, this tablet has similar specs to the Amazon Fire tablets. Build quality seems great for a 10 inch tablet that costs less than $100. The IPS screen is reasonably sharp and colorful (though slightly lower resolution than the 10" Amazon Fire tablet). It is fine for web surfing, email, and media streaming (videos, movies, music, etc). It is really too slow for playing fancier video games.

Speaker quality is mediocre (like with most phones or tablets), but there is an audio jack that you can use with headphones or external speakers (which I highly recommend for listening to music or watching movies).

32GB of storage is barely adequate if you like taking photos/videos or if you want to locally store songs and movies, but I like that there is a micro-SD card slot so you can add flash memory card.

I like that this tablet setup easily, unlike some other cheap Android tablets that I have tried. You can use your existing Google account or create a new one when you setup the tablet. The tablet runs a standard (though not the latest) Android operating system, which I think is much easier to use than the Amazon Fire operating system.

I like that they include a charging cable and charger, but I do not like that the tablet does not work with my phone's charger. My phone uses USB-C Power Delivery charging, which works with all other USB-C devices that I have tried. I have no idea why it does not work with this tablet.

I really do not like that this tablet does not get the monthly Android security patches from Google. I received this tablet in June 2022 and the latest security patch that is available from this manufacturer is from April 2021 (more than 1 year ago). Name brand Android devices should install the security patches within 1 or 2 months of when they are released, so using an Android device that is more than 1 year out-of-date is kind of risky. This device might be OK for watching movies or listening to music from name-brand streaming services, but I would not use it for any financial transactions (banking or credit card). Also beware of web surfing to any sketchy websites. Even using it for email is kind of iffy if you use the same email address for financial transactions.

2.5 stars, mostly because of the security updates issue.

I own a Google Pixel 6 smartphone with a USB-C port and no stereo audio port. I ordered these headphones because the product title says they will work with Google phones. These headphones do not work with my phone. They plug in to the USB-C port fine, but the phone does not recognize them. The product title says Google phones are supported and the product description says "universal compatibility with USB-C devices". Both statements are false. I own other USB-C headphones that work fine. 1 star.

I see Amazon selling a lot of products from this brand. I am now hesitant to order any of them.

This webcam installed plug-and-play on my Windows 10 PC. The Amazon product description says the camera has "real time autofocus", but I cannot get that to work. The instructions for the camera are terrible and don't say anything about autofocus. The instructions only say "manual focus HD lens" with no instructions on how to manually focus the lens. The lens ring is very small and slippery, so manually focusing the lens via the lens ring is very difficult. The microphone on the webcam is also mediocre with recordings sounding weak and muddy compared to other microphones that I have tried with this PC.

I wanted to like these headphones because good USB-C headphones are hard to find, this set is inexpensive, and I really like the carrying case that it comes with. Unfortunately, the sound quality is terrible with my Google Pixel 2 phone. The sound is very muddy and not clear at all; easily one of the worst headphones that I have ever tried. I have tried other USB-C headphones from Belkin and OnePlus that sound fine on my phone and USB-C stereo adapters also work fine, so the problem is these headphones. The product description says it is supposed to work with the Google Pixel 2 phone.  Maybe it works better with other phones, but this is the only USB-C phone that I can try.

I really wanted to like this camera. Construction quality is better than most budget-priced 4K action cameras. Price is much lower than GoPro. Battery life is great. Video quality is good for this price (but noticeably worse than GoPro and it lacks the 4K 60fps mode that GoPro has). Unfortunately, audio quality is poor.

A smartphone app is required to use much of the camera's functionality, including setting up the camera and all the wireless control features. I was able to download the app (a huge 75MB download to my Android phone). The app will not work until you create an account on Xiaomi's server in China. I am reluctant to send any of my personal information to an overseas corporation, but even when I tried to do it, I was unable to create the account, even after an hour of trying. The app does not work at all if I cannot login to the account.

A few more negatives about this camera. While the video quality is very good for this price level, audio recording quality is mediocre. This camera comes with no accessories in the box, just the camera, battery, brief instruction manual (more of the manual is in the app that I cannot use), and a charging cable (micro-USB, not USB-C like most modern devices). The camera uses a standard 1/4 inch tripod mount, but there is no GoPro-style action mount that would be much more sturdy and reliable if you are attaching the camera to a bicycle or helmet. There is no case to protect the camera from dirt or weather or use it underwater. Amazon does not sell any accessories either, so I don't know how to use this camera in an action situation. One battery is included in the box, but battery life is less than 2 hours and I always carry spares with my other action cameras. Again, Amazon does not sell spares.

Because of all these limitations, I can only give this camera 2 stars right now. Maybe if the app mysteriously starts working at some point and Amazon starts selling accessories to make the camera more usable, then I will consider reviewing the camera again.

These are big heavy headphones, but the large well-padded ear cups make them comfortable to me, even over glasses. The fold up design makes them reasonably portable for travel use.

If you can't use earbuds because of comfort or fit issues and you don't want to wear expensive headphones in a noisy environment like a public bus, then these may be good enough for you. If you're listening to music in a quiet environment (like in your home), I have to recommend spending a little more for much better sound quality from other products.

*** Update October 2021 ***
The ear cushions stay on very loosely, always was a problem, but it finally happened that I lost one somewhere. Now the whole unit is useless just for one foam earpiece. Stay away from this.

Pros

1. Excellent sound, with more clarity than the other Bluetooth earbuds I own. They are especially better for listening to music.

2. The earbuds and their case have a sleek, attractive design.

Cons

1. Each small ear piece operates separately. They are not attached to each other via a plastic-coated wire as is typically the case for earbuds. This means that, when I remove these earbuds from my ears, because there is no wire holding them securely around my neck, they must be carefully and consistently placed in their carrying case, and then either set in a safe, easily remembered location, or placed in my pants pocket. Neither option is desirable. It is extremely difficult to not get distracted and set down these earbuds in a random location, such that afterwards I have to waste a lot of time looking for them. And the problem with slipping them into a pocket is that there is a strong possibility I might accidentally leave them there, such that they end up in the washer and dryer and are ruined. In short, the risk of losing or destroying these earbuds is enormous!

2. Each ear piece must be turned ON/OFF separately, one after the other. This is a hassle.

3. The ON/OFF controls are extremely difficult to engage. You touch an ear piece and hold it for several seconds to turn each ear piece on or off. There is no button. The ear piece is somehow sensing the pressure of the touch of a fingertip. I frequently have great difficulty locating and pressing the exact spot required in order to turn these earbuds on or off. This is a major pain!

4. Volume is controlled the same way as the ON/OFF function, by magically managing to touch the earpiece in the exact, necessary location with the appropriate amount of fingertip pressure. It is very difficult to accomplish that, and the frustration of failing at this onerous task again and again is maddening!

For all of the above reasons, I wouldn’t recommend these earbuds to my worst enemy!

I received these earphones from Amazon Vine in early January, 2018. I liked the over-the-ears design. It makes the earphones far less likely to fall off when exercising. The sound quality is also excellent. I found its wireless bluetooth function quite handy for listening to music on my smartphone while walking, biking, lifting weights or doing calisthenics.

In short, as long as the battery could be charged, these sport earphones worked quite well. But suddenly, a few weeks ago, after only 7 months of use, the battery simply would no longer take a charge. The manual says that the battery should last through up to 300 charges, and there is absolutely no way that in only seven months I charged this device 300 times. It holds a charge well while the battery is working, much better than the other bluetooth earbuds that I have owned. So I could use it for up to five days without charging the battery. This means that, in seven months, I only charged the battery about 42-50 times, at most. This means the life of the battery was a mere 16% of what the manufacturer promised!

This is not a device in which the battery can be replaced. Therefore, once the battery dies, the earphones are worthless. Since the warranty is only for 90 days, there is no recourse with the manufacturer for replacing this device after that length of time.

The way that this product works is a good idea, but until the design includes the possibility of replacing the battery, the high price is simply not worth it. I will have to stick to cheap earbuds which are not such a hit to my pocketbook when their non-replaceable battery dies.
